BSc Electrical Engineering (Computer) · Semester VII · Module Data Storage and Analysis

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
• Understand database concepts and architecture

    File-based systems vs. DBMS, the ANSI-SPARC three-schema architecture, multi-user DBMS, and the database development life cycle.

  • Master the relational model

    Relations, tuples, attributes, domains, keys, entity and referential integrity constraints, schema vs. instance.

  • Design databases conceptually

    E-R modelling: entities, attributes, relationships, cardinality, participation, weak entities, and EER constructs (specialisation, generalisation, categories).

  • Map conceptual models to relational schemas

    The 7-step ER-to-relational mapping, the 9-step EER-to-relational mapping, and informal design guidelines.

  • Apply normalization

    Functional dependencies, Armstrong's axioms, closure, minimal covers, and the normal forms 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF.

  • Query databases with SQL

    DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, constraints) and DML (SELECT with joins, aggregates, GROUP BY, subqueries, EXISTS, UPDATE, INSERT, DELETE).

  • Understand storage and indexing

    Disk structure, file organisation (heap, sorted, hashed), dynamic and extendible hashing, and RAID levels.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text:
• Introduction

    File-based systems and their limitations; the database approach; DBMS components; ANSI-SPARC architecture; multi-user DBMS; development life cycle.

    Chapter 1

  • The Relational Model

    Data models; relations, tuples, attributes, domains; keys; entity and referential integrity; schema vs. instance.

    Chapter 2

  • Conceptual Database Design — E-R Modelling

    Entities, attributes, relationships; cardinality and participation; weak entities; EER concepts (subclasses, specialisation, generalisation, categories); attribute and relationship inheritance.

    Chapter 3

  • Logical Database Design

    The 7-step ER-to-relational mapping; the 9-step EER-to-relational mapping; informal design guidelines; functional dependencies; normalisation (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF).

    Chapter 4

  • Relational Algebra and Calculus

    Unary and binary operations; set-theoretic operations; joins; division; tuple and domain calculus; examples on the COMPANY database.

    Chapter 5

  • Structured Query Language (SQL)

    DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, constraints); DML (SELECT with joins, aggregates, subqueries, set operations, EXISTS, NULLs); INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.

    Chapter 6

  • Disk Storage, File Structures, and Hashing

    Disk storage devices; files of records; unordered, ordered, and hashed files; dynamic and extendible hashing; RAID technology.

    Chapter 7

Instructions (mock exam):

  • Time: 3 hours

docs.title: A1. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
Which of the following is not a limitation of file-based systems?

(a) data redundancy (b) data inconsistency (c) program-data dependence (d) support for concurrent access by multiple users

docs.title: A2. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
In the ANSI-SPARC three-schema architecture, the schema that describes the physical storage structure is the:

(a) external schema (b) conceptual schema (c) internal schema (d) view schema

docs.title: A3. Short answer [3]
docs.text: List three advantages of the database approach over file-based systems. For each, give one concrete example.

docs.title: A4. Short answer [3]
docs.text: Explain the difference between logical and physical data independence. Why is physical data independence easier to achieve than logical?

docs.title: B1. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
In a relation, a candidate key is:

(a) any attribute (b) a minimal superkey (c) a foreign key (d) the first attribute

docs.title: B2. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
The referential integrity constraint states that:

(a) every tuple has a unique primary key (b) a foreign key value must either be NULL or match a primary key value in the referenced relation (c) no attribute can contain NULLs (d) every relation must have at least one tuple

docs.title: B3. Short answer [3]
docs.text: Given a relation EMPLOYEE(emp_id, name, dept_id) and DEPARTMENT(dept_id, dept_name), identify a candidate key, a primary key, and a foreign key. Explain each choice.

docs.title: B4. Short answer [3]
docs.text: Distinguish between a relation schema and a relation instance. Give an example of each for the EMPLOYEE relation.

docs.title: C1. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
A weak entity is one that:

(a) has no attributes (b) cannot exist without a related owner entity (c) has only one attribute (d) has no primary key at all

docs.title: C2. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
In the EER model, generalisation is the process of:

(a) splitting a superclass into subclasses (b) combining subclasses into a superclass (c) adding more attributes to an entity (d) removing relationships

docs.title: C3. Short answer [4]
docs.text:
For the COMPANY database described below, draw a complete ER diagram:

  • EMPLOYEE (ssn, name, address, salary, sex, birth_date)
  • DEPARTMENT (dnumber, dname)
  • PROJECT (pnumber, pname, location)
  • Each department has exactly one manager (an employee) and controls many projects.
  • Each employee works in exactly one department and may work on many projects with a weekly hours attribute.
  • Each employee may have many dependents, each with name, sex, birth_date, and relationship.

State every cardinality ratio, participation constraint, and any weak entity.

docs.title: C4. Short answer [4]
docs.text:
Given an entity PERSON with subclasses STUDENT and EMPLOYEE, both of which can further have subclasses GRAD_STUDENT and STAFF:

  • Draw the EER diagram with specialisation/generalisation.
  • State whether the specialisation is disjoint or overlapping — justify your choice.
  • State whether it is total or partial — justify your choice.

docs.title: C5. Short answer [3]
docs.text: Explain attribute inheritance in the EER model. Give one example where inheritance is useful and one where it would be inappropriate.

docs.title: Section D — Logical Design and Normalisation (Ch 4) — 25 marks
D1. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
The third normal form (3NF) eliminates:

(a) partial dependencies on a candidate key (b) transitive dependencies on a candidate key (c) all functional dependencies (d) the need for a primary key

docs.title: D2. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
A relation is in BCNF if, for every non-trivial functional dependency \(X \to Y\):

(a) \(Y\) is a candidate key (b) \(X\) is a superkey (c) \(X \subseteq Y\) (d) \(Y \subseteq X\)

docs.title: D3. Short answer [4]
docs.text:
Map the following ER model to relational schemas (show all steps 1–7):

  • STUDENT (student_id, name, address — multivalued)
  • COURSE (course_id, title)
  • ENROLLMENT — M:N relationship between STUDENT and COURSE, with attribute grade
  • DEPENDENT — weak entity of STUDENT with attribute dep_name
  • PROFESSOR (prof_id, name) — each professor advises many students (1:N relationship with STUDENT)

Write the resulting CREATE TABLE statements (keys, foreign keys, and constraints).

docs.title: D4. Derivation [5]
docs.text:
Let \(R(A, B, C, D, E)\) with functional dependencies:

\[ AB \to C, \quad C \to D, \quad D \to E. \]
  1. Compute the closure of \(AB\).
  2. Identify all candidate keys of \(R\).
  3. Decompose \(R\) into 3NF using the synthesis algorithm.
  4. Is the decomposition also in BCNF? Justify.

docs.title: D5. Short answer [4]
docs.text:
Given \(R(A, B, C, D)\) with \(AB \to C\), \(C \to D\), and \(D \to A\):

  • Is \(R\) in 3NF? In BCNF? Justify.
  • If not in BCNF, decompose it and verify that the decomposition is lossless.

docs.title: D6. Short answer [3]
docs.text:
Explain the three informal design guidelines for relational databases:

  1. Semantics of attributes — why should each tuple represent one entity?
  2. Redundant information — what anomalies does it cause?
  3. NULL values — what problems do they introduce in joins?

Give one example of each.

docs.title: D7. Short answer [5]
docs.text:
Consider the relation:

EMPLOYEE_PROJECT(emp_id, emp_name, dept_name, proj_id, proj_name, hours)

where each employee works on one or more projects, emp_name and dept_name depend only on emp_id, and proj_name depends only on proj_id.

  1. List the functional dependencies.
  2. Identify all candidate keys.
  3. Normalise to 3NF.
  4. State one update anomaly that the original schema suffers from.

docs.title: Section E — Relational Algebra and Calculus (Ch 5) — 15 marks
E1. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
The division operation \(R \div S\) in relational algebra returns:

(a) the Cartesian product of \(R\) and \(S\) (b) tuples of \(R\) that match all tuples of \(S\) on the common attributes (c) tuples of \(R\) that match some tuples of \(S\) (d) the union of \(R\) and \(S\)

docs.title: E2. Short answer [4]
docs.text:
Using the COMPANY database from Section C:

  • Dnumber of the department with the highest-paid manager.
  • Names of employees who work on projects in more than 2 departments.
  • Names of employees who work on all projects.

Express each query in relational algebra. You may assume the relations EMPLOYEE(ssn, name, salary, dno), DEPARTMENT(dnumber, mgr_ssn), PROJECT(pnumber, dnum), WORKS_ON(essn, pno).

docs.title: E3. Short answer [4]
docs.text:
Express the following query in both relational algebra and tuple relational calculus:

"Find the names of departments in which every employee earns more than 30,000."

docs.title: E4. Short answer [5]
docs.text:
Given relations \(R(A, B)\) and \(S(B, C)\), write queries that return:

  1. The natural join \(R \bowtie S\).
  2. The left outer join \(R ⟕ S\).
  3. Pairs \((a, c)\) such that \(B\) in \(R\) is not in \(S\).
  4. All \(A\) values that appear in \(R\) with at least two different \(B\) values.

Express each in relational algebra.

docs.title: F1. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
Which SQL clause is evaluated last (i.e., after GROUP BY and HAVING)?

(a) SELECT (b) WHERE (c) ORDER BY (d) FROM

docs.title: F2. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
The difference between WHERE and HAVING is that:

(a) WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after grouping (b) HAVING filters rows before grouping, WHERE filters groups after grouping (c) they are equivalent (d) WHERE only works with aggregates

docs.title: F3. Short answer [4]
docs.text:
Using the COMPANY database, write the SQL for each query:

  1. Names of employees whose salary is above the department average.
  2. Names of departments with more than 5 employees and an average salary of at least 40,000.
  3. Names of employees who do not work on any project.
  4. Names of employees who work on all projects.

docs.title: F4. Short answer [4]
docs.text:
Write the DDL to create the EMPLOYEE and DEPARTMENT tables from the COMPANY database:

  • EMPLOYEE(ssn, name, salary, dno) — dno references DEPARTMENT
  • DEPARTMENT(dnumber, dname, mgr_ssn) — mgr_ssn references EMPLOYEE

Include PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, NOT NULL, and UNIQUE constraints. Handle the circular reference appropriately.

docs.title: F5. Short answer [3]
docs.text:
Explain the difference between:

  • EXISTS and IN.
  • UNION and UNION ALL.

Give one query where each choice matters.

docs.title: Section G — Storage and Hashing (Ch 7) — 10 marks
G1. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
RAID level 1 is:

(a) striping without redundancy (b) mirroring (c) bit-level striping with parity (d) block-level striping with distributed parity

docs.title: G2. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
Extendible hashing differs from static hashing in that it:

(a) stores all records in one bucket (b) grows and shrinks the directory dynamically as records are added or removed (c) uses a linked list of overflow blocks (d) requires a pre-allocated file of fixed size

docs.title: G3. Short answer [3]
docs.text:
Compare static hashing, dynamic hashing, and extendible hashing on:

  • overflow handling,
  • directory size,
  • growth behaviour.

docs.title: G4. Short answer [3]
docs.text:
Explain the RAID 0, 1, 5 levels:

  • How does each distribute data across disks?
  • What is the trade-off between performance, redundancy, and cost?

docs.title: Grading rubric
docs.text:
Band Marks A 90–100 B 75–89 C 60–74 F < 60

Common error checks:

  • Missing foreign key in a mapping exercise: −2.
  • Mapping a multivalued attribute into the same relation instead of a separate table: −3.
  • Confusing 3NF with BCNF: −2.
  • Natural join used where a theta join is needed: −2.
  • Aggregate function used in WHERE instead of HAVING: −2.
  • Missing NOT NULL on a primary key in DDL: −1.
  • Confusing RAID 1 with RAID 5: −2.

docs.title: Course description
docs.text: This course provides a solid foundation in database systems — both the theoretical principles and the practical skills needed to design, implement, and query a relational database. It follows the canonical lifecycle: from understanding requirements, through conceptual and logical design, to physical design and SQL implementation. It closes with the storage-level concerns of disk files and hashing.

docs.title: Course objectives and competences
docs.text:
Upon completion of this course, students will have gained knowledge of database system concepts and the ability to:

  1. Understand user requirements and views.
  2. Analyse existing and future data-processing needs.
  3. Develop an enterprise data model that reflects the organisation's fundamental business rules.
  4. Develop and refine the conceptual data model, including all entities, relationships, attributes, and business rules.
  5. Integrate and merge database views into a conceptual model.
  6. Apply normalisation techniques.
  7. Derive a physical design from the logical design taking into account application, hardware, operating system, and data communications network requirements.

docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Contact hours: 2 lecture + 1 tutorial · Home study: ~5 h

Coverage: manual file handling systems · traditional file-based systems · database approach · DBMS · components of the DBMS environment · database development life cycle · common uses · ANSI-SPARC architecture · multi-user DBMS.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
1. Explain the limitations of file-based systems that motivate the database approach.
  2. Describe the components of a DBMS environment.
  3. Draw the ANSI-SPARC three-schema architecture and explain data independence.
  4. List the phases of the database development life cycle (DBLC).

docs.title: 1.1 File-based systems and their limitations
docs.text:
Before DBMSs, data was stored in separate files managed by application programs.

Limitations (Elmasri §1.2):

Limitation Description Data redundancy Same data stored in multiple files Data inconsistency Different copies diverge over time Program-data dependence File format defined in the program — changing the format requires changing every program Difficulty of access New queries require new programs Data isolation Data scattered across files in different formats Integrity problems Constraints enforced only in programs, not in data Atomicity problems A crash can leave the data half-updated Concurrent-access anomalies Multiple users can corrupt data if not coordinated Security problems Access control at file level only

Example. A university has separate files for students, courses, and enrolments. A student's name may appear in all three; updating it in one file but not the others creates inconsistency.

docs.title: 1.2 The database approach
docs.text:
Definition (Elmasri §1.3)

A database is an organised collection of structured data. A DBMS is software that manages and controls access to the database.

The database approach has these properties:

  • Self-describing: the database stores its own schema (catalog or data dictionary).
  • Insulation: programs are independent of data format (program–data independence).
  • Multiple views: different users see different subsets.
  • Sharing: multiple users and programs share one data store.
  • Transaction support: atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability (ACID).
  • Integrity constraints: enforced by the DBMS.

docs.title: 1.3 Components of a DBMS environment
docs.text:
+-----------------------------------------------+
|  Users: end users, application programmers, DBA |
+-----------------------------------------------+
|  Application programs and queries              |
+-----------------------------------------------+
|  DBMS: query processor, storage manager         |
+-----------------------------------------------+
|  Stored data                                    |
+-----------------------------------------------+

Five components (Elmasri §1.5):

  1. Hardware — physical storage.
  2. Software — the DBMS itself, plus application programs.
  3. Data — the database and the catalog.
  4. Procedures — instructions for using the system.
  5. People — end users, application programmers, DBAs, database designers.

docs.title: 1.4 ANSI-SPARC three-schema architecture
docs.text:
ANSI-SPARC (Elmasri §2.2)

The three-level architecture separates:

  1. External (view) level — how users see the data.
  2. Conceptual (logical) level — the community-wide logical structure.
  3. Internal (physical) level — how data is stored.
Users ─► External schemas (views)
                │
                ▼  logical data independence
        Conceptual schema (community view)
                │
                ▼  physical data independence
        Internal schema (storage details)
                │
                ▼
           Stored database

Data independence:

  • Logical data independence — change the conceptual schema without changing the external schemas.
  • Physical data independence — change the internal schema without changing the conceptual schema.

docs.title: 1.5 The database development life cycle (DBLC)
docs.text:
Phase Description 1. Requirements analysis Interview users, produce a requirements specification 2. Conceptual design Build the ER/EER model, independent of any DBMS 3. Choice of DBMS Evaluate vendors against the requirements 4. Logical design Map the conceptual model to a relational schema; normalise 5. Physical design Choose file structures, indexes, storage layout 6. Implementation Create the schema in the DBMS, load data 7. Testing Validate against requirements 8. Operation and maintenance Monitor, tune, evolve

The DBLC is iterative — discovery in later phases often forces refinement of earlier ones.

docs.title: 1.6 Multi-user DBMS
docs.text:
A multi-user DBMS supports concurrent access by many users. Key concerns:

  • Concurrency control — prevent simultaneous updates from corrupting data.
  • Transaction management — atomic commits, rollback on failure.
  • Recovery — restore a consistent state after a crash.
  • Security — authenticate users, authorise access.
  • Views — present tailored subsets of the data.

docs.text:
1. List five limitations of file-based systems.
  2. What is a DBMS? Name four of its key features.
  3. Draw the ANSI-SPARC three-schema architecture and explain each level.
  4. Distinguish logical from physical data independence.
  5. List the phases of the database development life cycle.

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text:
Click to reveal
  1. Data redundancy, inconsistency, program-data dependence, difficulty of access, concurrent-access anomalies.
  2. A DBMS is software that manages and controls access to a database. Key features: self-describing, program-data independence, multiple views, ACID transactions.
  3. (See diagram above.)
  4. Logical: change conceptual schema without changing external views. Physical: change internal schema without changing conceptual schema.
  5. Requirements analysis, conceptual design, choice of DBMS, logical design, physical design, implementation, testing, operation and maintenance.

docs.title: Learning outcomes

  2. Identify superkeys, candidate keys, primary keys, and foreign keys.
  3. State and apply the entity-integrity and referential-integrity constraints.

docs.title: 2.1 Data models
docs.text:
A data model is a set of concepts for describing data, relationships, semantics, and constraints.

Category Examples Conceptual ER model, EER model (Chapter 3) Logical Relational, object-oriented, object-relational Physical Files, indexes (Chapter 7)

The relational model is the dominant logical model — nearly every commercial DBMS implements it.

docs.title: 2.2 The relational model
docs.text:
Definition (Elmasri §3.1, Codd 1970)

A relation is a set of tuples over a schema \(R(A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n)\), where each attribute \(A_i\) takes values from a domain \(D_i\).

Formally, a relation \(r\) on schema \(R\) is a subset of the Cartesian product \(D_1 \times D_2 \times \cdots \times D_n\).

Key properties (Codd's requirements):

  • Each tuple is unique (a relation is a set of tuples).
  • Tuples are unordered.
  • Attributes are unordered (although column order may be presented).
  • Each attribute value is atomic (1NF — see Chapter 4).

docs.title: 2.3 Terminology
docs.text: Formal term Informal equivalent Relation Table Tuple Row Attribute Column Domain Data type (permitted values) Degree Number of attributes Cardinality Number of tuples

docs.title: 2.4 Keys
docs.text:
Term Definition Superkey Any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a tuple Candidate key A minimal superkey (no attribute can be removed) Primary key A chosen candidate key Foreign key Attribute(s) in one relation that match a primary key in another

Example. In EMPLOYEE(emp_id, ssn, name, dept_id):

  • Superkeys: emp_id, ssn, (emp_id, ssn), (emp_id, name), …
  • Candidate keys: emp_id, ssn.
  • Primary key: emp_id (chosen).
  • Foreign key: dept_id references DEPARTMENT.

docs.title: 2.5 Relational constraints
docs.text:
Two key constraints (Elmasri §3.2):

Entity-integrity constraint

No primary-key attribute may be NULL. Every tuple must have a unique, non-null identifier.

Referential-integrity constraint

For a foreign key \(FK\) in relation \(R_1\) referencing primary key \(PK\) in \(R_2\): for every tuple in \(R_1\), either \(FK\) is NULL, or \(FK\) matches a \(PK\) value in \(R_2\).

Referential-action options:

Action On DELETE / UPDATE of referenced key RESTRICT / NO ACTION Reject CASCADE Propagate the change SET NULL Set the foreign key to NULL SET DEFAULT Set the foreign key to its default

docs.title: 2.6 Schema vs. instance
docs.text:
Term Definition Schema The structure — relation names, attribute names, types, constraints (rarely changes) Instance The current set of tuples (changes constantly)

Example schema:

CREATE TABLE EMPLOYEE (
    emp_id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name     VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    dept_id  INTEGER,
    FOREIGN KEY (dept_id) REFERENCES DEPARTMENT(dept_id)
);

Example instance:

emp_id name dept_id 101 Alice 10 102 Bob 20 103 Carol 10

docs.title: 2.7 Quiz
docs.text:
1. Define relation, tuple, attribute, and domain.
  2. What is the difference between a superkey, a candidate key, and a primary key?
  3. State the entity-integrity and referential-integrity constraints.
  4. Give one example of a schema and one of an instance.
  5. Distinguish the four referential actions (RESTRICT, CASCADE, SET NULL, SET DEFAULT).

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text:
Click to reveal
  1. Relation = table; tuple = row; attribute = column; domain = set of permitted values for an attribute.
  2. Superkey uniquely identifies a tuple; candidate key is a minimal superkey; primary key is a chosen candidate key.
  3. Entity: no primary-key attribute is NULL. Referential: foreign key is NULL or matches a primary-key value in the referenced relation.
  4. (See §2.6.)
  5. RESTRICT: reject. CASCADE: propagate. SET NULL: nullify. SET DEFAULT: replace with default value.

docs.title: Chapter 4 — Logical Database Design and Normalisation
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Coverage: ER-to-relational mapping (7 steps) · EER-to-relational mapping (2 extra steps) · informal design guidelines · functional dependencies · normal forms 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
1. Apply the 7-step ER-to-relational mapping algorithm.
  2. Apply the 2 extra steps for EER constructs (specialisation, categories).
  3. State and use Armstrong's axioms to compute closures and minimal covers.
  4. Normalise a schema to 3NF and BCNF; verify decomposition quality.

docs.title: 4.1 The 7-step ER-to-relational mapping (Elmasri §9.1)
docs.text:
Step 1 — Regular entity types. Each regular entity becomes a relation. Include all simple attributes. Choose one key as primary key.

Step 2 — Weak entity types. Each weak entity becomes a relation. Include the owner's primary key as a foreign key. The primary key is (owner key, partial key).

Step 3 — Binary 1:1 relationships. Include the primary key of one side as a foreign key in the other side. Prefer the side with total participation.

Step 4 — Binary 1:N relationships. Include the primary key of the "1" side as a foreign key in the "N" side.

Step 5 — Binary M:N relationships. Create a new relation with foreign keys to both sides. Primary key is the combination of both foreign keys. Add any relationship attributes.

Step 6 — Multivalued attributes. Create a new relation with the attribute and the owner's primary key. Primary key is (owner key, attribute).

Step 7 — N-ary relationships. Create a new relation with foreign keys to all participants.

docs.title: 4.1.1 EER extra steps (Elmasri §9.2)
docs.text:
Step 8 — Specialisation / generalisation. Four options:

Option Description When to use 8A Multiple relations (superclass + subclasses) Any specialisation 8B Multiple relations (subclasses only) Total, disjoint 8C Single relation with a type attribute Disjoint, no subclass-specific attributes 8D Single relation with multiple type attributes Overlapping

Step 9 — Categories. Create one relation per subclass, and a new relation for the category that includes the primary key of each participant, plus a type discriminator.

docs.title: Worked example 4.1 — mapping the COMPANY database
docs.text:
Input ER. (From Chapter 3.)

Step 1 — regular entities.

CREATE TABLE EMPLOYEE (
    ssn        CHAR(9) PRIMARY KEY,
    name       VARCHAR(50),
    address    VARCHAR(100),
    salary     DECIMAL(10,2),
    sex        CHAR(1),
    birth_date DATE
);

CREATE TABLE DEPARTMENT (
    dnumber    INT PRIMARY KEY,
    dname      VARCHAR(50) UNIQUE
);

CREATE TABLE PROJECT (
    pnumber    INT PRIMARY KEY,
    pname      VARCHAR(50),
    location   VARCHAR(50)
);

Step 3 — 1:1 MANAGES. Put mgr_ssn (foreign key to EMPLOYEE) in DEPARTMENT.

ALTER TABLE DEPARTMENT ADD COLUMN mgr_ssn CHAR(9),
    ADD FOREIGN KEY (mgr_ssn) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(ssn);

Step 4 — 1:N WORKS_FOR and CONTROLS. Add foreign keys on the "N" side.

ALTER TABLE EMPLOYEE ADD COLUMN dno INT,
    ADD FOREIGN KEY (dno) REFERENCES DEPARTMENT(dnumber);

ALTER TABLE PROJECT ADD COLUMN dnum INT,
    ADD FOREIGN KEY (dnum) REFERENCES DEPARTMENT(dnumber);

Step 5 — M:N WORKS_ON.

CREATE TABLE WORKS_ON (
    essn CHAR(9),
    pno  INT,
    hours DECIMAL(3,1),
    PRIMARY KEY (essn, pno),
    FOREIGN KEY (essn) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(ssn),
    FOREIGN KEY (pno)  REFERENCES PROJECT(pnumber)
);

Step 6 — multivalued attribute locations of DEPARTMENT.

CREATE TABLE DEPT_LOCATIONS (
    dnumber   INT,
    dlocation VARCHAR(50),
    PRIMARY KEY (dnumber, dlocation),
    FOREIGN KEY (dnumber) REFERENCES DEPARTMENT(dnumber)
);

Step 2 — weak entity DEPENDENT.

CREATE TABLE DEPENDENT (
    essn           CHAR(9),
    dependent_name VARCHAR(50),
    sex            CHAR(1),
    birth_date     DATE,
    relationship   VARCHAR(20),
    PRIMARY KEY (essn, dependent_name),
    FOREIGN KEY (essn) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(ssn)
);

Result: seven relations — EMPLOYEE, DEPARTMENT, PROJECT, WORKS_ON, DEPT_LOCATIONS, DEPENDENT (and the EER subclasses to be added in Step 8).

docs.title: 4.2 Informal design guidelines (Elmasri §14.1)
docs.text:
Three red flags in a relational design:

  1. Attribute semantics — each attribute should describe a single, clearly-defined property of the entity. Mixing semantics (e.g., a phone attribute that sometimes holds a home number, sometimes a work number) confuses joins.
  2. Redundant information — duplicating data in tuples causes update anomalies (insertion, deletion, modification).
  3. NULL values — excessive NULLs waste space and complicate joins; they also make constraints and aggregates hard to interpret.

Spurious tuples — decompositions that produce extra rows on join indicate a bad design. A lossless-join decomposition is one that avoids spurious tuples.

docs.title: 4.3 Functional dependencies (Elmasri §14.2)
docs.text:
Definition

A functional dependency (FD) \(X \to Y\) on relation \(R\) holds if, for every two tuples \(t_1, t_2\) with \(t_1[X] = t_2[X]\), we also have \(t_1[Y] = t_2[Y]\).

Armstrong's axioms (sound and complete):

  • Reflexivity: if \(Y \subseteq X\), then \(X \to Y\).
  • Augmentation: if \(X \to Y\), then \(XZ \to YZ\).
  • Transitivity: if \(X \to Y\) and \(Y \to Z\), then \(X \to Z\).

Derived rules:

  • Union: \(X \to Y, X \to Z \Rightarrow X \to YZ\).
  • Decomposition: \(X \to YZ \Rightarrow X \to Y, X \to Z\).
  • Pseudotransitivity: \(X \to Y, WY \to Z \Rightarrow WX \to Z\).

Closure. The closure \(X^+\) of \(X\) under \(F\) is the set of all attributes functionally determined by \(X\).

Minimal cover. A set \(F_{\min}\) equivalent to \(F\) with:

  • No redundant attributes (every dependency is needed).
  • No redundant attributes on the left side.
  • RHS has a single attribute per dependency.

docs.title: Worked example 4.2 — closure and minimal cover
docs.text:
Given. \(R(A,B,C,D,E)\) with \(F = \{AB \to C,\ C \to D,\ D \to E\}\).

Compute \((AB)^+\):

  • \(AB\) (initial)
  • \(+ C\) (from \(AB \to C\))
  • \(+ D\) (from \(C \to D\))
  • \(+ E\) (from \(D \to E\))

So \((AB)^+ = \{A, B, C, D, E\}\) — \(AB\) is a superkey.

Is \(AB\) a candidate key? Check \((A)^+ = \{A\}\) and \((B)^+ = \{B\}\) — neither is a superkey. \(AB\) is a candidate key. It is the only candidate key (nothing else determines \(A\) or \(B\)).

Minimal cover of \(F\): \(F\) is already minimal — no dependency can be removed without losing equivalence, and the left sides are single-attribute or minimal.

docs.title: 4.4.1 1NF — first normal form
docs.text:
1NF

Every attribute value is atomic — no sets, lists, or nested relations.

Fix: move multivalued attributes into a separate relation.

docs.title: 4.4.2 2NF — second normal form
docs.text:
2NF

In 1NF, and every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on every candidate key (no partial dependency on part of a key).

Fix: decompose so partial dependencies go to their own relations.

docs.title: 4.4.3 3NF — third normal form
docs.text:
3NF

In 2NF, and no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on any candidate key. Equivalently, for every non-trivial FD \(X \to Y\): \(X\) is a superkey, or \(Y\) is a prime attribute.

docs.title: 4.4.4 BCNF — Boyce-Codd normal form
docs.text:
BCNF

For every non-trivial FD \(X \to Y\): \(X\) is a superkey.

BCNF is stricter than 3NF: it removes all FDs based on non-superkey determinants, even if the RHS is prime.

docs.title: Worked example 4.3 — 3NF synthesis
docs.text:
Given. \(R(A,B,C,D,E)\) with \(F = \{AB \to C,\ C \to D,\ D \to E\}\).

Step 1 — minimal cover. \(F\) is minimal.

Step 2 — combine FDs with the same LHS. None shared.

Step 3 — create a relation per dependency:

  • \(R_1(A, B, C)\)
  • \(R_2(C, D)\)
  • \(R_3(D, E)\)

Step 4 — add a relation for any candidate key not covered. \(AB\) is covered by \(R_1\).

Result. \(R_1, R_2, R_3\) — in 3NF (each FD has a superkey or prime RHS) and dependency-preserving.

Is it BCNF? No. \(C \to D\) has \(C\) not a superkey of \(R_2\). Decompose \(R_2\) into \(R_2'(C)\) — but that loses the dependency. So 3NF is the best we can do while preserving dependencies.

docs.title: 4.5 Practical use of normal forms
docs.text:
• 3NF is the practical target for most OLTP systems — it removes redundancy while preserving dependencies.
  • BCNF removes additional redundancy but may lose dependency preservation (may require join to check a dependency).
  • Denormalisation is sometimes used in data warehouses — deliberately introduce redundancy for query performance.

docs.title: 4.6 Quiz
docs.text:
1. List the 7 steps of the ER-to-relational mapping.
  2. Map an ER model with a weak entity to relations.
  3. State Armstrong's three axioms.
  4. Compute the closure of \(AB\) given \(AB \to C, C \to D, D \to E\).
  5. Distinguish 3NF from BCNF. Give an example of a relation that is in 3NF but not in BCNF.

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text:
Click to reveal
  1. Regular entities → weak entities → 1:1 → 1:N → M:N → multivalued → n-ary.
  2. Weak entity gets a relation with (owner PK, partial key) as PK.
  3. Reflexivity, augmentation, transitivity.
  4. \(AB^+ = \{A,B,C,D,E\}\).
  5. 3NF allows \(Y\) prime in \(X \to Y\); BCNF requires \(X\) superkey. Example: \(R(A,B,C)\) with \(AB \to C, C \to B\). Candidate keys: \(AB, AC\). \(C \to B\) has \(C\) not a superkey, \(B\) prime → 3NF but not BCNF.

    ADD FOREIGN KEY (mgr_ssn) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(ssn);

Step 4 — 1:N WORKS_FOR and CONTROLS. Add foreign keys on the "N" side.

ALTER TABLE EMPLOYEE ADD COLUMN dno INT,
    ADD FOREIGN KEY (dno) REFERENCES DEPARTMENT(dnumber);

ALTER TABLE PROJECT ADD COLUMN dnum INT,
    ADD FOREIGN KEY (dnum) REFERENCES DEPARTMENT(dnumber);

Step 5 — M:N WORKS_ON.

CREATE TABLE WORKS_ON (
    essn CHAR(9),
    pno  INT,
    hours DECIMAL(3,1),
    PRIMARY KEY (essn, pno),
    FOREIGN KEY (essn) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(ssn),
    FOREIGN KEY (pno)  REFERENCES PROJECT(pnumber)
);

Step 6 — multivalued attribute locations of DEPARTMENT.

CREATE TABLE DEPT_LOCATIONS (
    dnumber   INT,
    dlocation VARCHAR(50),
    PRIMARY KEY (dnumber, dlocation),
    FOREIGN KEY (dnumber) REFERENCES DEPARTMENT(dnumber)
);

Step 2 — weak entity DEPENDENT.

CREATE TABLE DEPENDENT (
    essn           CHAR(9),
    dependent_name VARCHAR(50),
    sex            CHAR(1),
    birth_date     DATE,
    relationship   VARCHAR(20),
    PRIMARY KEY (essn, dependent_name),
    FOREIGN KEY (essn) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(ssn)
);

Result: seven relations — EMPLOYEE, DEPARTMENT, PROJECT, WORKS_ON, DEPT_LOCATIONS, DEPENDENT (and the EER subclasses to be added in Step 8).

docs.title: 4.2 Informal design guidelines (Elmasri §14.1)
docs.text:
Three red flags in a relational design:

  1. Attribute semantics — each attribute should describe a single, clearly-defined property of the entity. Mixing semantics (e.g., a phone attribute that sometimes holds a home number, sometimes a work number) confuses joins.
  2. Redundant information — duplicating data in tuples causes update anomalies (insertion, deletion, modification).
  3. NULL values — excessive NULLs waste space and complicate joins; they also make constraints and aggregates hard to interpret.

Spurious tuples — decompositions that produce extra rows on join indicate a bad design. A lossless-join decomposition is one that avoids spurious tuples.

docs.title: 4.3 Functional dependencies (Elmasri §14.2)
docs.text:
Definition

A functional dependency (FD) \(X \to Y\) on relation \(R\) holds if, for every two tuples \(t_1, t_2\) with \(t_1[X] = t_2[X]\), we also have \(t_1[Y] = t_2[Y]\).

Armstrong's axioms (sound and complete):

  • Reflexivity: if \(Y \subseteq X\), then \(X \to Y\).
  • Augmentation: if \(X \to Y\), then \(XZ \to YZ\).
  • Transitivity: if \(X \to Y\) and \(Y \to Z\), then \(X \to Z\).

Derived rules:

  • Union: \(X \to Y, X \to Z \Rightarrow X \to YZ\).
  • Decomposition: \(X \to YZ \Rightarrow X \to Y, X \to Z\).
  • Pseudotransitivity: \(X \to Y, WY \to Z \Rightarrow WX \to Z\).

Closure. The closure \(X^+\) of \(X\) under \(F\) is the set of all attributes functionally determined by \(X\).

Minimal cover. A set \(F_{\min}\) equivalent to \(F\) with:

  • No redundant attributes (every dependency is needed).
  • No redundant attributes on the left side.
  • RHS has a single attribute per dependency.

docs.title: Worked example 4.2 — closure and minimal cover
docs.text:
Given. \(R(A,B,C,D,E)\) with \(F = \{AB \to C,\ C \to D,\ D \to E\}\).

Compute \((AB)^+\):

  • \(AB\) (initial)
  • \(+ C\) (from \(AB \to C\))
  • \(+ D\) (from \(C \to D\))
  • \(+ E\) (from \(D \to E\))

So \((AB)^+ = \{A, B, C, D, E\}\) — \(AB\) is a superkey.

Is \(AB\) a candidate key? Check \((A)^+ = \{A\}\) and \((B)^+ = \{B\}\) — neither is a superkey. \(AB\) is a candidate key. It is the only candidate key (nothing else determines \(A\) or \(B\)).

Minimal cover of \(F\): \(F\) is already minimal — no dependency can be removed without losing equivalence, and the left sides are single-attribute or minimal.

docs.title: 4.4.1 1NF — first normal form
docs.text:
1NF

Every attribute value is atomic — no sets, lists, or nested relations.

Fix: move multivalued attributes into a separate relation.

docs.title: 4.4.2 2NF — second normal form
docs.text:
2NF

In 1NF, and every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on every candidate key (no partial dependency on part of a key).

Fix: decompose so partial dependencies go to their own relations.

docs.title: 4.4.3 3NF — third normal form
docs.text:
3NF

In 2NF, and no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on any candidate key. Equivalently, for every non-trivial FD \(X \to Y\): \(X\) is a superkey, or \(Y\) is a prime attribute.

docs.title: 4.4.4 BCNF — Boyce-Codd normal form
docs.text:
BCNF

For every non-trivial FD \(X \to Y\): \(X\) is a superkey.

BCNF is stricter than 3NF: it removes all FDs based on non-superkey determinants, even if the RHS is prime.

docs.title: Worked example 4.3 — 3NF synthesis
docs.text:
Given. \(R(A,B,C,D,E)\) with \(F = \{AB \to C,\ C \to D,\ D \to E\}\).

Step 1 — minimal cover. \(F\) is minimal.

Step 2 — combine FDs with the same LHS. None shared.

Step 3 — create a relation per dependency:

  • \(R_1(A, B, C)\)
  • \(R_2(C, D)\)
  • \(R_3(D, E)\)

Step 4 — add a relation for any candidate key not covered. \(AB\) is covered by \(R_1\).

Result. \(R_1, R_2, R_3\) — in 3NF (each FD has a superkey or prime RHS) and dependency-preserving.

Is it BCNF? No. \(C \to D\) has \(C\) not a superkey of \(R_2\). Decompose \(R_2\) into \(R_2'(C)\) — but that loses the dependency. So 3NF is the best we can do while preserving dependencies.

docs.title: 4.5 Practical use of normal forms
docs.text:
• 3NF is the practical target for most OLTP systems — it removes redundancy while preserving dependencies.
  • BCNF removes additional redundancy but may lose dependency preservation (may require join to check a dependency).
  • Denormalisation is sometimes used in data warehouses — deliberately introduce redundancy for query performance.

docs.title: 4.6 Quiz
docs.text:
1. List the 7 steps of the ER-to-relational mapping.
  2. Map an ER model with a weak entity to relations.
  3. State Armstrong's three axioms.
  4. Compute the closure of \(AB\) given \(AB \to C, C \to D, D \to E\).
  5. Distinguish 3NF from BCNF. Give an example of a relation that is in 3NF but not in BCNF.

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text:
Click to reveal
  1. Regular entities → weak entities → 1:1 → 1:N → M:N → multivalued → n-ary.
  2. Weak entity gets a relation with (owner PK, partial key) as PK.
  3. Reflexivity, augmentation, transitivity.
  4. \(AB^+ = \{A,B,C,D,E\}\).
  5. 3NF allows \(Y\) prime in \(X \to Y\); BCNF requires \(X\) superkey. Example: \(R(A,B,C)\) with \(AB \to C, C \to B\). Candidate keys: \(AB, AC\). \(C \to B\) has \(C\) not a superkey, \(B\) prime → 3NF but not BCNF.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Elmasri & Navathe, §9.1–§9.2, §14.1–§14.6.
  • Silberschatz et al., §7.1–§7.7.

docs.title: Chapter 5 — Relational Algebra and Calculus
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Coverage: unary and binary relational-algebra operations · set-theoretic operations · joins · division · tuple and domain calculus · COMPANY examples.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
1. Express queries in the fundamental relational-algebra operations.
  2. Use joins, outer joins, and division correctly.
  3. Translate between relational algebra, tuple relational calculus, and domain relational calculus.

docs.title: 5.1 Relational algebra
docs.text:
Definition (Elmasri §6.1)

Relational algebra is a procedural query language: each query is a sequence of operations on relations, producing a new relation.

Six fundamental operations: \(\sigma, \pi, \cup, -, \times, \rho\).

docs.title: 5.1.1 Unary operations
docs.text:
• Selection \(\sigma_{\text{condition}}(R)\) — keeps tuples satisfying the condition.
  • Projection \(\pi_{A_1, \ldots, A_k}(R)\) — keeps only the listed attributes (duplicates removed).
  • Rename \(\rho_{S}(R)\) — renames a relation or its attributes.

docs.title: 5.1.2 Set-theoretic operations
docs.text:
For \(R\) and \(S\) with the same schema (union-compatible):

  • Union \(R \cup S\).
  • Intersection \(R \cap S\).
  • Set difference \(R - S\).

docs.title: 5.1.3 Cartesian product
docs.text: \(R \times S\) — every tuple of \(R\) paired with every tuple of \(S\).

docs.title: 5.1.4 Joins
docs.text: Join Symbol Meaning Theta join \(R \bowtie_\theta S\) Cartesian product filtered by \(\theta\) Equijoin \(R \bowtie_{A=B} S\) Theta join with equality Natural join \(R \bowtie S\) Equijoin on all common attributes, duplicate columns removed Left outer join \(R ⟕ S\) Keeps unmatched tuples from \(R\), pads \(S\) with NULLs Right outer join \(R ⟖ S\) Symmetric Full outer join \(R ⟗ S\) Union of both

docs.title: 5.1.5 Division
docs.text: \(R \div S\) (with \(S\)'s attributes a subset of \(R\)'s) returns the tuples \(t\) of \(R\) such that for every tuple \(s\) in \(S\), the combined tuple \((t, s)\) is in \(R\). Used for "for all" queries.

docs.title: Worked example 5.1 — COMPANY queries in relational algebra
docs.text:
Schema.

  • EMPLOYEE(ssn, name, salary, dno)
  • DEPARTMENT(dnumber, dname, mgr_ssn)
  • PROJECT(pnumber, pname, dnum)
  • WORKS_ON(essn, pno, hours)

Q1. Names of employees who work on the 'ProductX' project.

\[ \pi_{\text{name}}\bigl(\text{EMPLOYEE} \bowtie \text{WORKS\_ON} \bowtie \pi_{\text{pnumber}}\bigl(\sigma_{\text{pname}=\text{'ProductX'}}(\text{PROJECT})\bigr)\bigr) \]

Q2. Names of employees who do not work on any project.

\[ \pi_{\text{name}}\bigl(\text{EMPLOYEE}\bigr) - \pi_{\text{name}}\bigl(\text{EMPLOYEE} \bowtie \text{WORKS\_ON}\bigr) \]

Q3. Names of employees who work on all projects.

\[ \pi_{\text{name}}\Bigl(\text{EMPLOYEE} \bowtie \bigl(\pi_{\text{essn, pno}}(\text{WORKS\_ON}) \div \pi_{\text{pnumber}}(\text{PROJECT})\bigr)\Bigr) \]

docs.title: Worked example 5.2 — tuple relational calculus
docs.text:
Query (Q1 above) in TRC:

\[ \{ e.\text{name} \mid \text{EMPLOYEE}(e) \land \exists\, w \in \text{WORKS\_ON} \;\exists\, p \in \text{PROJECT} \; (w.\text{essn} = e.\text{ssn} \land w.\text{pno} = p.\text{pnumber} \land p.\text{pname} = \text{'ProductX'}) \} \]

Query (Q3 above) in TRC:

\[ \{ e.\text{name} \mid \text{EMPLOYEE}(e) \land \forall\, p \in \text{PROJECT}\; \exists\, w \in \text{WORKS\_ON} \; (w.\text{essn} = e.\text{ssn} \land w.\text{pno} = p.\text{pnumber}) \} \]

Why TRC is more declarative. The user writes "what" (the conditions), not "how" (the order of operations). Both RA and TRC express the same queries (relational completeness) — every RA expression is expressible in safe TRC and vice versa.

docs.title: Worked example 5.3 — domain relational calculus
docs.text:
Query (Q1) in DRC:

\[ \{\, n \mid \exists\, s, a, d \;\; \text{EMPLOYEE}(s, n, a, d) \land \exists\, p, h \;\; \text{WORKS\_ON}(s, p, h) \land \exists\, pn, dn \;\; \text{PROJECT}(p, \text{'ProductX'}, dn) \,\} \]

Difference from TRC. DRC quantifies over domain values rather than tuples; the same query looks similar but the variables are attribute values.

docs.title: 5.2 Quiz
docs.text:
1. Express "names of employees who work on projects in department 5" in relational algebra.
  2. Express "departments with every employee earning > 30,000" in relational algebra.
  3. Write a TRC formula for "employees who manage a department."
  4. What is division in relational algebra used for? Give one example.
  5. Why does relational algebra produce only safe expressions automatically, while calculus needs safety restrictions?

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text:
Click to reveal
  1. \(\pi_{\text{name}}(\text{EMPLOYEE} \bowtie \text{WORKS\_ON} \bowtie \sigma_{\text{dnum}=5}(\text{PROJECT}))\).
  2. \(\pi_{\text{dno}}(\text{EMPLOYEE}) - \pi_{\text{dno}}(\sigma_{\text{salary} < 30000}(\text{EMPLOYEE}))\).
  3. \(\{e.\text{name} \mid \text{EMPLOYEE}(e) \land \exists\, d \in \text{DEPARTMENT} \; (d.\text{mgr\_ssn} = e.\text{ssn})\}\).
  4. "For all" queries — e.g., employees who work on all projects.
  5. RA is built from operations that always produce finite relations from finite inputs; calculus allows expressions that range over infinite domains, so safety (domain independence) is needed.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Elmasri & Navathe, §6.1–§6.6, §8.6 (calculus).
  • Silberschatz et al., §2.6, §6.1.
  • Ramakrishnan & Gehrke, §4.2–§4.3.

docs.title: Chapter 6 — Structured Query Language (SQL)
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Coverage: objectives of SQL · DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP) · DML (SELECT, joins, aggregates, subqueries, set operations, EXISTS, NULLs) · INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
1. Create, alter, and drop databases and tables with constraints.
  2. Write SELECT queries with WHERE, ORDER BY, DISTINCT, aliases.
  3. Use joins, aggregates, GROUP BY, HAVING, and subqueries correctly.
  4. Modify data with INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE while respecting constraints.

docs.title: 6.1 Objectives of SQL
docs.text:
SQL was designed to be:

  • Declarative — specify what you want, not how to get it.
  • Universal — the same syntax works on every major DBMS.
  • Standardised — ANSI/ISO standard since 1986 (SQL-86, SQL-92, SQL:1999, SQL:2003, SQL:2008, SQL:2011, …).
  • Non-procedural — queries express sets of rows, not loops.

Two sublanguages:

  • DDL (Data Definition Language) — define schema.
  • DML (Data Manipulation Language) — query and modify data.

docs.title: 6.2 DDL — CREATE, ALTER, DROP
docs.text:
CREATE DATABASE COMPANY;

CREATE TABLE DEPARTMENT (
    dnumber INT PRIMARY KEY,
    dname   VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    mgr_ssn CHAR(9)
);

CREATE TABLE EMPLOYEE (
    ssn       CHAR(9) PRIMARY KEY,
    name      VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    salary    DECIMAL(10, 2) CHECK (salary >= 0),
    dno       INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (dno) REFERENCES DEPARTMENT(dnumber)
);

ALTER TABLE DEPARTMENT
    ADD FOREIGN KEY (mgr_ssn) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(ssn)
    ON DELETE SET NULL ON UPDATE CASCADE;

DROP TABLE EMPLOYEE;

Constraints summary:

Constraint Meaning PRIMARY KEY Uniquely identifies each tuple; implies NOT NULL FOREIGN KEY Referential integrity UNIQUE All values distinct (NULL allowed) NOT NULL No NULL allowed CHECK Boolean condition on each tuple DEFAULT Default value

Referential actions:

  • ON DELETE RESTRICT — reject the delete (default in many DBMS).
  • ON DELETE CASCADE — delete dependent tuples.
  • ON DELETE SET NULL — set foreign key to NULL.
  • ON DELETE SET DEFAULT — set to default.

docs.title: 6.3.1 Basic form
docs.text:
SELECT   DISTINCT dno
FROM     EMPLOYEE
WHERE    salary > 40000
ORDER BY name ASC;

Logical evaluation order:

  1. FROM
  2. WHERE
  3. GROUP BY
  4. HAVING
  5. SELECT
  6. DISTINCT
  7. ORDER BY

(This is why an aggregate cannot appear in WHERE — aggregation has not happened yet.)

docs.title: 6.3.2 Joins
docs.text:
Explicit inner join:

SELECT e.name, d.dname
FROM   EMPLOYEE e INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT d ON e.dno = d.dnumber;

Left outer join (keep employees without a department):

SELECT e.name, d.dname
FROM   EMPLOYEE e LEFT JOIN DEPARTMENT d ON e.dno = d.dnumber;

docs.title: 6.3.3 Aggregates and grouping
docs.text:
SELECT   dno, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary, COUNT(*) AS n_employees
FROM     EMPLOYEE
GROUP BY dno
HAVING   COUNT(*) > 5;

Rules.

  • Aggregate functions: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX.
  • Every non-aggregated column in SELECT must appear in GROUP BY.
  • WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after grouping.

docs.title: 6.3.4 Subqueries
docs.text:
Scalar subquery (one value):

SELECT name
FROM   EMPLOYEE
WHERE  salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM EMPLOYEE);

Correlated subquery:

SELECT name
FROM   EMPLOYEE e
WHERE  salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE dno = e.dno);

EXISTS:

SELECT d.dname
FROM   DEPARTMENT d
WHERE  EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM EMPLOYEE e WHERE e.dno = d.dnumber);

IN vs. EXISTS. IN compares a value to a subquery result; EXISTS tests whether the subquery produces any rows. Performance depends on the DBMS and the indexes.

docs.title: 6.3.5 Set operations
docs.text:
SELECT ssn FROM EMPLOYEE
UNION
SELECT ssn FROM MANAGER;

SELECT ssn FROM EMPLOYEE
INTERSECT
SELECT ssn FROM MANAGER;

SELECT ssn FROM EMPLOYEE
EXCEPT              -- MINUS in Oracle
SELECT ssn FROM MANAGER;

UNION removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps them (faster).

docs.title: 6.3.6 NULL handling
docs.text:
• NULL is unknown, not empty and not zero.
  • NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, not TRUE.
  • Use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL for comparison.
  • Arithmetic with NULL yields NULL.
  • COUNT(column) ignores NULLs; COUNT(*) counts rows.

docs.title: 6.3.7 String operations
docs.text:
SELECT name
FROM   EMPLOYEE
WHERE  name LIKE 'Sm%'             -- starts with Sm
   OR  name LIKE '_mith'           -- _ matches one character
   OR  SUBSTRING(name, 1, 3) = 'Ali';

docs.title: Worked example 6.1 — six SQL queries
docs.text:
Schema. EMPLOYEE(ssn, name, salary, dno), DEPARTMENT(dnumber, dname, mgr_ssn), PROJECT(pnumber, pname, dnum), WORKS_ON(essn, pno, hours).

Q1. Names of employees earning more than the average.

SELECT name FROM EMPLOYEE
WHERE  salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM EMPLOYEE);

Q2. Departments with more than 5 employees and an average salary of at least 40,000.

SELECT   d.dname
FROM     DEPARTMENT d JOIN EMPLOYEE e ON e.dno = d.dnumber
GROUP BY d.dnumber, d.dname
HAVING   COUNT(*) > 5 AND AVG(e.salary) >= 40000;

Q3. Names of employees who do not work on any project.

SELECT name FROM EMPLOYEE e
WHERE  NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM WORKS_ON w WHERE w.essn = e.ssn);

Q4. Names of employees who work on all projects.

SELECT name FROM EMPLOYEE e
WHERE  NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT pnumber FROM PROJECT
    EXCEPT
    SELECT pno      FROM WORKS_ON WHERE essn = e.ssn
);

Q5. For each department, the name of its highest-paid employee.

SELECT d.dname, e.name, e.salary
FROM   EMPLOYEE e
       JOIN DEPARTMENT d ON e.dno = d.dnumber
WHERE  e.salary = (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE dno = d.dnumber);

Q6. Update salaries — give every employee in department 5 a 10% raise.

UPDATE EMPLOYEE
SET    salary = salary * 1.10
WHERE  dno = 5;

docs.title: 6.4 INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
docs.text:
INSERT INTO EMPLOYEE (ssn, name, salary, dno)
VALUES ('999999999', 'Alice', 45000, 5);

UPDATE EMPLOYEE SET salary = salary * 1.05 WHERE dno = 5;

DELETE FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE ssn = '999999999';

Constraint violation examples:

  • Insert with duplicate primary key → UNIQUE violation.
  • Insert with non-existent dno → FOREIGN KEY violation.
  • Delete a department that still has employees → FOREIGN KEY violation (unless ON DELETE CASCADE).
  • Update a primary key that other rows reference → FOREIGN KEY violation (unless ON UPDATE CASCADE).

docs.title: 6.5 Quiz
docs.text:
1. Write the DDL for EMPLOYEE and DEPARTMENT with all necessary constraints.
  2. What is the logical evaluation order of a SELECT query?
  3. Explain the difference between WHERE and HAVING.
  4. Write a query that finds employees who earn more than their department average.
  5. What is the difference between IN and EXISTS? Give an example where each is preferred.

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text:
Click to reveal
  1. (See §6.2.)
  2. FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY.
  3. WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after grouping.
  4. (Q6.1 above, using correlated subquery.)
  5. IN checks against a set of values; EXISTS tests for existence of matching rows. EXISTS is often faster with correlated subqueries and can short-circuit; IN is simpler when the subquery returns a static list.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Elmasri & Navathe, §4.1–§4.5, §5.1–§5.4.
  • Silberschatz et al., §3.1–§3.10, §4.1–§4.2.
  • SQLBolt (sqlbolt.com) for hands-on practice.

docs.title: Chapter 7 — Disk Storage, File Structures, and Hashing
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Coverage: disk storage devices · files of records · unordered, sorted, and hashed files · dynamic and extendible hashing · RAID.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
1. Describe the physical structure of a magnetic disk and the cost of block access.
  2. Compare file organisations: heap, sorted, hashed.
  3. Explain static, dynamic, and extendible hashing.
  4. Describe RAID levels 0–6 and their trade-offs.

docs.title: 7.1 Disk storage devices
docs.text:
A magnetic hard disk consists of platters, each divided into tracks, each track into sectors. A block is the unit of disk I/O (typically 4 KB).

Access cost:

\[ T_{\text{access}} = T_{\text{seek}} + T_{\text{rotational}} + T_{\text{transfer}} \] Component Typical value Seek time 3–10 ms Rotational latency ~4 ms (7200 RPM) Transfer time ~0.1 ms per 4 KB

Seek time dominates — disk scheduling algorithms (FCFS, SSTF, SCAN) are designed to reduce total head movement.

SSDs have no moving parts: constant-time random access, but finite write cycles and asymmetric read/write performance.

docs.title: 7.2 Files of records
docs.text:
A file is a sequence of records stored on disk. Each record consists of fields (attributes).

Fixed-length records — all records the same size; direct access by (record_number × record_size).

Variable-length records — records differ in size; use a slotted-page layout with a slot directory and record offsets.

docs.title: 7.3.1 Unordered (heap) file
docs.text:
Records inserted at the end. New records go wherever there is free space.

  • Insert: \(O(1)\) (if space is available).
  • Search by key: \(O(b)\) where \(b\) is the number of blocks — full scan.

docs.title: 7.3.2 Sorted (sequential) file
docs.text:
Records kept in key order.

  • Search by key: \(O(\log_2 b)\) — binary search over blocks.
  • Insert: \(O(b)\) — shifting.

docs.title: 7.3.3 Hashed file
docs.text:
A hash function \(h(k)\) maps the key to a bucket (block or set of blocks).

  • Search by key: \(O(1)\) on average.
  • Range queries: \(O(b)\) — hashing destroys order.

docs.title: 7.4 Static hashing
docs.text:
A fixed number of buckets \(M\) is allocated. Each key \(k\) hashes to bucket \(h(k) \bmod M\).

Overflow problem. If a bucket fills, overflow blocks are chained. As the file grows, overflow chains lengthen, and search degrades from \(O(1)\) to \(O(n)\).

The fix: dynamic hashing.

docs.title: 7.5 Dynamic hashing
docs.text: Two main variants:

docs.title: 7.5.1 Extendible hashing
docs.text:
Uses a directory (an array of pointers to buckets) indexed by the first \(d\) bits of the hash value.

  • Global depth \(d\) — number of bits used by the directory.
  • Local depth \(d_i\) — number of bits used by bucket \(i\).
  • When a bucket overflows, split it and increment its local depth; double the directory if needed.

Properties.

  • \(O(1)\) search in the directory, plus one block access.
  • Directory doubles at most \(\log_2 n\) times for \(n\) records.
  • No overflow chains (except transiently during splits).

docs.title: 7.5.2 Linear hashing
docs.text:
Grows the file one bucket at a time — no directory. Uses a split pointer and a level counter. Splits happen when the load factor exceeds a threshold.

Properties.

  • Simpler than extendible hashing (no directory).
  • Splits are incremental, so the file grows smoothly.
  • Slightly slower search (need to check the split state).

docs.title: 7.6 RAID
docs.text:
RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) combines multiple disks for performance, redundancy, or both.

Level Technique Redundancy Performance Cost RAID 0 Striping (no redundancy) None Fastest Low RAID 1 Mirroring Full Fast read, slower write 2× storage RAID 5 Block-level striping with distributed parity 1-disk failure Good read, slower write 1 disk overhead RAID 6 Striping with double parity 2-disk failure Good read, slower write 2 disks overhead

RAID 0 is fast but has no fault tolerance — one disk failure loses everything.

RAID 1 duplicates every write; storage efficiency 50%, but read can be served from either copy.

RAID 5 distributes parity across all disks; reading is fast, writing has a "write penalty" (read-modify-write of parity). Rebuild after a failure is slow.

RAID 6 is RAID 5 with two parity blocks per stripe — survives two simultaneous failures. Often used for large arrays (e.g., > 12 TB).

docs.title: Worked example 7.1 — choosing a RAID level
docs.text:
Scenario A — a database server with high read/write ratio and tolerance for 1-disk failure.

Choice: RAID 5 or RAID 10. RAID 5 offers good capacity efficiency; RAID 10 (mirror + stripe) gives better write performance but 50% storage overhead.

Scenario B — a backup server, sequential writes dominate, capacity matters.

Choice: RAID 6. Two-disk redundancy, good capacity efficiency, write performance is acceptable.

Scenario C — a scratch/scratch-adjacent server with maximum speed, no durability requirement.

Choice: RAID 0. Fastest, but any failure loses data — acceptable only if the data is regenerable.

Scenario D — a small server with only two disks.

Choice: RAID 1. The only level that gives redundancy with two disks.

docs.title: 7.7 Quiz
docs.text:
1. List the three components of disk access time and rank them by typical magnitude.
  2. Compare heap, sorted, and hashed files on search and insert cost.
  3. What problem does dynamic hashing solve that static hashing cannot?
  4. Explain extendible hashing — what is the role of the directory and global/local depth?
  5. Choose a RAID level for a video-editing workstation and justify.

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text:
Click to reveal
  1. Seek (~3–10 ms) > rotational (~4 ms) > transfer (~0.1 ms).
  2. Heap: O(b) search, O(1) insert. Sorted: O(log b) search, O(b) insert. Hashed: O(1) search, O(1) insert.
  3. Static hashing uses a fixed number of buckets; as the file grows, overflow chains lengthen and search degrades. Dynamic hashing grows the bucket count.
  4. Directory is an array of pointers indexed by the top \(d\) bits of the hash; local depth controls how many bits distinguish a given bucket's keys; when a bucket overflows, its local depth increments and the directory may double.
  5. RAID 0 for maximum sequential throughput (scratch space); RAID 5 if resilience is required and budget is limited.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

1. Explain **why file-based systems fail** at scale, with five concrete limitations. 2. Define a **DBMS** and describe its five components of the environment. 3. Draw and explain the **ANSI-SPARC three-schema architecture** and the two types of data independence. 4. Describe the **database development life cycle** (DBLC) and the role of each phase. 5. Identify the **five components** of a multi-user DBMS and the trade-offs between them.

docs.title: 1.1 — File-Based Systems
docs.text:
Definition

A file-based system stores data in separate files, each managed by its own application program. There is no centralized control over the data.

???+ info "The canonical structure" 
Application 1  ───►  File 1 (Students)
Application 2  ───►  File 2 (Courses)
Application 3  ───►  File 3 (Enrollments)
Each application has its own view of the data — and its own copy. !!! warning "The fundamental problem" Data is **owned by applications**, not by the enterprise. Any change to the data format requires updating every application that touches it.

docs.title: 1.2 — Five Limitations of File-Based Systems
docs.text:
1. Data redundancy

The same fact is stored in multiple files. A student's name appears in Students, Enrollments, and Grades.

???+ note "2. Data inconsistency" Different copies diverge over time. Updating the name in one file but not the others creates **contradictions**. ???+ note "3. Program-data dependence" The file format is defined **inside the program**. Changing the format (adding a column, changing a length) requires editing every program. ???+ note "4. Difficulty of access" New questions ("Which students took CS301 in 2023?") require writing **new programs**, not just new queries. ???+ note "5. Concurrency and atomicity" Multiple users can corrupt data. A crash mid-update leaves the data **inconsistent**.

docs.title: 1.2 — Concrete Example of Redundancy
docs.text: A university with three applications Application File Fields Registrar Students.dat id, name, address, dept Payroll Payroll.dat id, name, dept, salary Library Loans.dat id, name, book, date !!! warning "Three copies of `name` and `dept`" - **Update anomaly:** when a student changes their name, three files must be updated — if any is missed, the data becomes inconsistent. - **Insertion anomaly:** you cannot record a new department until a student joins it. - **Deletion anomaly:** deleting a student's payroll record also deletes their `name` and `dept` — even if the registrar still needs them. These three anomalies — update, insertion, deletion — are the concrete symptoms of redundancy. The database approach does not just "store data in one place"; it eliminates the structural causes of these anomalies. That is the real argument for normalization (Chapter 4).

docs.title: 1.3 — The Database Approach
docs.text:
Definition (Elmasri §1.3)

A database is an organized collection of structured data. A DBMS is software that manages and controls access to the database.

???+ info "Key properties of the database approach" | Property | Meaning | |---|---| | **Self-describing** | The database stores its own schema (catalog / data dictionary) | | **Insulation** | Programs are independent of data format | | **Multiple views** | Different users see different subsets | | **Sharing** | Multiple users and programs share one store | | **Transaction support** | ACID properties | | **Integrity constraints** | Enforced by the DBMS, not the program | !!! tip "The key insight" Data is a **shared corporate resource**. Applications come and go; data persists. The DBMS is the layer that lets data outlive applications.

docs.title: 1.4 — DBMS Environment: Five Components
docs.text:
Five components (Elmasri §1.5) 
┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  People: users, programmers, DBAs,       │
│          designers                       │
├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Procedures: instructions for using      │
│              the system                  │
├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Software: DBMS + application programs   │
├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Data: the database + the catalog        │
├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Hardware: storage, CPU, network         │
└──────────────────────────────────────────┘
!!! warning "The people component is not an afterthought" The DBA (Database Administrator) is responsible for: - **Schema design** and evolution. - **Security** (who can access what). - **Performance tuning** (indexes, statistics). - **Backup and recovery**. - **Capacity planning**.

docs.title: 1.5 — Functions of a DBMS
docs.text: What the DBMS actually does Function Description Data storage Persistent, structured, at scale Data retrieval Query processing and optimization Transaction management ACID: atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability Concurrency control Multiple users without corruption Recovery Restore a consistent state after a crash Security Authentication and authorization Integrity Enforce constraints (keys, references) Catalog Metadata about the schema   ???+ note "ACID in one line each"     - **Atomicity:** a transaction is all-or-nothing.     - **Consistency:** a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another.     - **Isolation:** concurrent transactions do not see each other's intermediate states.     - **Durability:** a committed transaction survives a crash.

docs.title: 1.6 — ANSI-SPARC Three-Schema Architecture
docs.text:
The three levels (Elmasri §2.2) 
External schema 1     External schema 2     External schema 3
     (view)                 (view)                (view)
           \                  |                  /
            \                 |                 /
             ─────►  Conceptual schema  ◄─────
                      (community view)
                          |
                          |
                          ▼
                     Internal schema
                    (storage details)
                          |
                          ▼
                     Stored database
???+ note "The three schemas" - **External (view) level** — what each user sees. - **Conceptual (logical) level** — the enterprise-wide logical structure. - **Internal (physical) level** — how data is stored. The three-schema architecture is the single most important design idea in databases. It is what makes data independence possible. Every modern DBMS implements it, even though the internal schema is often hidden from users.

docs.title: 1.7 — Data Independence
docs.text:
Logical data independence

The ability to change the conceptual schema without changing the external schemas.

Example: add a phone_number column to EMPLOYEE — applications that don't select it are unaffected.

???+ abstract "Physical data independence" The ability to change the **internal schema** without changing the **conceptual schema**. *Example:* change an index from B-tree to hash — queries written against the conceptual schema still work. !!! tip "Which is harder?" **Logical data independence is harder** to achieve because changes to the conceptual schema can affect queries in subtle ways. Physical data independence is "automatic" — the query processor chooses the physical access path.

docs.title: 1.8 — Database Languages
docs.text: The three languages of a DBMS Language Purpose Example statement DDL Define and modify the schema CREATE TABLE ... DML Query and modify the data SELECT ..., INSERT ... DCL Control access GRANT SELECT ON ... TO alice ???+ info "DDL is compiled, DML is interpreted" - DDL statements store **metadata** in the catalog. - DML statements are **compiled** into a query plan, then **executed**. - This is why the query processor has two stages: compilation and runtime.

docs.title: 1.9 — Database Development Life Cycle
docs.text: Eight phases Phase Output 1. Requirements analysis Requirements specification 2. Conceptual design ER / EER model 3. Choice of DBMS Vendor/product decision 4. Logical design Relational schema, normalized 5. Physical design Indexes, file structures, partitioning 6. Implementation Schema in the DBMS, data loaded 7. Testing Validated against requirements 8. Operation and maintenance Monitoring, tuning, evolution   !!! warning "The DBLC is iterative"     Design flaws discovered in later phases force refinement of earlier ones. Most real projects iterate 2–3 times through the design phases.

docs.title: 1.10 — Requirements Analysis
docs.text:
What goes into requirements
  • Data requirements — what entities, attributes, relationships.
  • Functional requirements — what operations (queries, updates).
  • Non-functional requirements — performance, security, availability.
???+ info "Techniques" - **Interviews** with stakeholders. - **Observation** of existing workflows. - **Analysis of existing documents** (forms, reports). - **Prototyping** — mock-ups to clarify requirements. !!! tip "The cost of bad requirements" Errors in requirements are the **most expensive to fix** — they propagate through every downstream phase. A 10× cost multiplier per phase is typical (Boehm's curve).

docs.title: 1.11 — Multi-User DBMS
docs.text: What changes when there are many users? Concern Why it matters Concurrency control Simultaneous updates can corrupt data Transaction management Commit/rollback on failure Recovery Restore consistency after a crash Security Authenticate, authorize Views Present tailored subsets Performance Scale with user count   ???+ note "The concurrency problem in one line"     Two transactions reading and writing the same data can produce a state **no serial execution would produce** — a *race condition* at the database level.     !!! tip "Isolation levels"     SQL standard defines four isolation levels (READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE). Higher isolation = fewer anomalies but less concurrency. This is the classic trade-off in multi-user DBMS.

docs.title: 1.12 — Common Uses of Database Systems
docs.text: Where databases appear Domain Example system Banking Account balances, transactions, loans Airlines Reservations, schedules, crew Universities Students, courses, grades, faculty E-commerce Products, orders, inventory, customers Healthcare Patients, records, prescriptions Telecommunications Call records, subscriptions, billing Social networks Users, posts, friendships, likes   !!! tip "Two patterns"     - **OLTP (Online Transaction Processing)** — many small, fast transactions. Banking, e-commerce.     - **OLAP (Online Analytical Processing)** — few large, complex queries. Data warehouses, business intelligence.

docs.title: Chapter 1 — key takeaways
docs.text: **1.** File-based systems fail because of **redundancy, inconsistency, program-data dependence, difficulty of access, and concurrency problems** — leading to update/insertion/deletion anomalies.     **2.** A **DBMS** is the software layer between users and data, providing storage, retrieval, transactions, concurrency, recovery, security, and integrity.     **3.** The **ANSI-SPARC** three-schema architecture separates **external** (views), **conceptual** (enterprise), and **internal** (physical) levels — enabling data independence.     **4.** **Logical data independence** is harder to achieve than physical because conceptual changes can ripple through queries.     **5.** The **DBLC** is an iterative eight-phase process; requirements analysis is the most consequential phase.     **6.** A **multi-user DBMS** adds concurrency control, transactions, recovery, and security — each with its own trade-offs.

docs.title: Next — Chapter 2
docs.text:
The Relational Model.

- Data models (conceptual, logical, physical). - **Relations**, **tuples**, **attributes**, **domains**. - **Keys**: superkey, candidate, primary, foreign. - **Entity-integrity** and **referential-integrity** constraints. - **Schema** vs. **instance**. Chapter 1 described what a DBMS *is*. Chapter 2 describes the **data model** that almost every DBMS implements.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text: 1. Classify the three types of **data models** (conceptual, logical, physical).     2. Define a **relation** formally and identify its components: tuples, attributes, domains, degree, cardinality.     3. Distinguish **superkey**, **candidate key**, **primary key**, and **foreign key**.     4. State and apply the **entity-integrity** and **referential-integrity** constraints.     5. Distinguish a **schema** from an **instance**.

docs.title: 2.1 — Data Models
docs.text:
Definition

A data model is a collection of concepts for describing data, relationships, semantics, and constraints.

???+ info "Three categories" | Category | Purpose | Examples | |---|---|---| | **Conceptual** | High-level, user-oriented | ER model, EER model (Chapter 3) | | **Logical** | DBMS-implementable | Relational, object-oriented, object-relational | | **Physical** | Storage-level | Files, indexes, page layouts (Chapter 7) | !!! tip "Each model has its own purpose" - Conceptual models are for **communication** with users. - Logical models are for **implementation**. - Physical models are for **performance**.

docs.title: 2.2 — The Relational Model
docs.text:
Definition (Codd 1970; Elmasri §3.1)

A relation \(r\) over schema \(R(A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n)\) is a subset of the Cartesian product of domains \(D_1 \times D_2 \times \cdots \times D_n\).

???+ info "What this means in practice" - A relation is a **set of tuples** — each tuple belongs to exactly one combination of domain values. - The **order** of tuples is irrelevant. - Each attribute value is **atomic** — no nested relations, no sets. !!! warning "Codd's requirements" - **No duplicate tuples** — a relation is a set, not a multiset. - **No ordering of tuples** — mathematically, there is no "first" tuple. - **No ordering of attributes** — although practical DBMSes fix a presentation order.

docs.title: 2.3 — Terminology
docs.text: The formal/informal mapping Formal Informal Example Relation Table EMPLOYEE Tuple Row (101, 'Alice', 50000, 10) Attribute Column name Domain Data type + constraints INTEGER, VARCHAR(50) Degree Number of columns 4 Cardinality Number of rows 1,000 ???+ info "The informal terms are fine for conversation" "Table", "row", and "column" are used informally everywhere — including in SQL documentation. "Relation", "tuple", and "attribute" are used in the formal theory and in query optimization.

docs.title: 2.4 — A Relation Instance
docs.text: Example: EMPLOYEE relation emp_id ssn name salary dept_id 101 111-22-3333 Alice 50,000 10 102 222-33-4444 Bob 60,000 20 103 333-44-5555 Carol 55,000 10 104 444-55-6666 David 45,000 20 105 555-66-7777 Eve 70,000 30 ???+ info "Vocabulary check" - **Degree** = 5 (five attributes). - **Cardinality** = 5 (five tuples). - **Domain of `salary`** = non-negative integers (or a DECIMAL type with a range). - **Primary key** = `emp_id`. Walk through this table slowly. Ask: what would happen if we allowed duplicate tuples? Then the "relation as set" property breaks, and operations like union, difference, and division become ambiguous. This is why SQL's default (bag semantics) is a departure from Codd's pure model, requiring DISTINCT.

docs.title: 2.5 — Keys: The Four Levels
docs.text:
Superkey

Any set of attributes \(K \subseteq R\) such that no two tuples agree on \(K\).

???+ abstract "Candidate key" A **minimal** superkey — no proper subset of $K$ is a superkey. ???+ abstract "Primary key" A **chosen** candidate key (the "official" identifier). ???+ abstract "Foreign key" An attribute (or set) in relation $R_1$ that references the **primary key** of another relation $R_2$. !!! tip "The hierarchy" Every **candidate key** is a **superkey**, but not vice versa. The primary key is one of the candidate keys. Foreign keys reference primary keys.

docs.title: 2.6 — Keys: Worked Example
docs.text: Given relation EMPLOYEE(emp_id, ssn, name, dept_id) Key type Example Why Superkey (emp_id), (ssn), (emp_id, ssn), (emp_id, name), (ssn, name) All uniquely identify a tuple Candidate key emp_id, ssn Minimal — removing any attribute loses uniqueness Primary key emp_id Chosen as the official identifier Foreign key dept_id References DEPARTMENT.dept_id ???+ warning "Not every superkey is a candidate key" `(emp_id, ssn)` is a superkey, but **not** a candidate key — because `emp_id` alone is already a superkey. The minimal ones are `emp_id` and `ssn`.

docs.title: 2.7 — Entity-Integrity Constraint
docs.text:
Entity-integrity constraint (Elmasri §3.2)

No primary-key attribute may be NULL. Every tuple must have a unique, non-null identifier.

???+ info "Why this is necessary" If a primary key could be NULL: - Multiple tuples could have NULL primary keys (NULL = NULL is unknown, not true). - The tuple would have no identifier. - Foreign keys referencing it would be ambiguous. ???+ warning "NULL is not a value" In SQL, NULL means "unknown" or "does not exist". NULL = NULL evaluates to **UNKNOWN**, not TRUE. This is why you use `IS NULL`, not `= NULL`.

docs.title: 2.8 — Referential-Integrity Constraint
docs.text:
Referential-integrity constraint (Elmasri §3.2)

For a foreign key \(FK\) in \(R_1\) referencing primary key \(PK\) in \(R_2\):

For every tuple \(t_1 \in R_1\), either: - \(t_1[FK]\) is NULL, or - there exists a tuple \(t_2 \in R_2\) with \(t_2[PK] = t_1[FK]\).

???+ note "What it prevents" **Dangling references.** Without the constraint, `EMPLOYEE.dept_id = 99` could exist even though no `DEPARTMENT` with `dept_id = 99` exists. !!! tip "The NULL allowance" A foreign key **may be NULL** — this represents "no reference" (e.g., a new employee not yet assigned to a department). But it must not point to a non-existent primary key.

docs.title: 2.9 — Referential Actions
docs.text: What happens on DELETE / UPDATE of the referenced key? Action Effect on the foreign key RESTRICT / NO ACTION Reject the operation CASCADE Delete / update the referencing tuple SET NULL Set the foreign key to NULL SET DEFAULT Set the foreign key to its default   ???+ info "Example: `DEPARTMENT` is deleted"     | Action | Result |     |---|---|     | RESTRICT | Delete fails — departments with employees cannot be deleted |     | CASCADE | Every employee in the department is also deleted |     | SET NULL | Employees' `dept_id` becomes NULL |     | SET DEFAULT | Employees' `dept_id` moves to a default department |     !!! warning "CASCADE is dangerous"     A single `DELETE FROM DEPARTMENT WHERE dept_id = 10` could delete hundreds of employees. Use CASCADE only when the relationship is **compositional** (the dependent cannot exist independently).

docs.title: 2.10 — Schema vs Instance
docs.text:
Schema vs instance Term Definition Changes Schema The structure — relation names, attribute names, types, constraints Rarely Instance The current set of tuples Constantly ???+ info "Example schema" 
CREATE TABLE EMPLOYEE (
    emp_id  INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name    VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    salary  DECIMAL(10,2) CHECK (salary >= 0),
    dept_id INTEGER,
    FOREIGN KEY (dept_id) REFERENCES DEPARTMENT(dept_id)
);
This is the **schema** — defined once, changed rarely. ???+ info "Example instance" | emp_id | name | salary | dept_id | |:---:|---|---:|---:| | 101 | Alice | 50,000 | 10 | | 102 | Bob | 60,000 | 20 | The **instance** changes with every insert, update, delete.

docs.title: 2.11 — Schema Notation
docs.text:
Formal notation

A relation schema is written:

\[ R(A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n) \]

with underlined primary key:

\[ \text{EMPLOYEE}(\underline{\text{emp\_id}}, \text{ssn}, \text{name}, \text{salary}, \text{dept\_id}) \] ???+ info "Foreign keys are shown with arrows" $$ \text{EMPLOYEE}(\underline{\text{emp\_id}}, \text{name}, \text{salary}, \text{dept\_id} \to \text{DEPARTMENT}) $$ !!! tip "This notation is the basis for everything in Chapter 4" ER-to-relational mapping (Chapter 4) produces exactly this notation. Normalization (Chapter 4) operates on these schemas.

docs.title: 2.12 — Relational Algebra Preview
docs.text: What operations does the model support? Operation Symbol Purpose Selection \(\sigma\) Filter tuples Projection \(\pi\) Select columns Union \(\cup\) Combine two relations Difference \(-\) Tuples in one but not other Cartesian product \(\times\) Every pairing Join \(\bowtie\) Combine on matching values   !!! tip "Chapter 5 develops these in full"     For now, understand that the relational model is not just data structures — it comes with a **query algebra**.
