That is what makes it uniquely powerful.

docs.title: Worked example 2.1 — Identify all key types
docs.text:
Problem:

Given:

STUDENT(student_id, ssn, name, dept, advisor_id)
COURSE(course_id, title, credits)
ENROLL(student_id, course_id, grade, semester)

Identify superkeys, candidate keys, primary keys, and foreign keys.

???+ note "**STUDENT**" - **Candidate keys:** `student_id`, `ssn`. - **Primary key:** `student_id`. - **Foreign key:** `advisor_id` → `STUDENT.student_id`. ??? info "**COURSE**" - **Candidate keys:** `course_id`. - **Primary key:** `course_id`. ??? info "**ENROLL**" - **Candidate key:** `(student_id, course_id, semester)` — because a student can take the same course in different semesters. - **Primary key:** `(student_id, course_id, semester)`. - **Foreign keys:** `student_id` → `STUDENT`, `course_id` → `COURSE`. ??? success "**Conclusion.**" Every table has exactly one primary key; foreign keys establish references; **composite keys** (ENROLL) arise when a single attribute is insufficient.

docs.title: Worked example 2.2 — Detect a constraint violation
docs.text:
Problem:

Given:

EMPLOYEE(emp_id, name, dept_id)   -- dept_id → DEPARTMENT
DEPARTMENT(dept_id, dname)

Current state:

EMPLOYEE emp_id name dept_id 1 Alice 10 2 Bob 20 3 Carol 99 DEPARTMENT dept_id dname 10 Sales 20 Engineering

Which constraint is violated?

???+ note "**Step 1 — check entity integrity.**" All `emp_id` values are non-NULL and unique → **satisfied**. ??? info "**Step 2 — check referential integrity.**" - `Alice → 10`: 10 exists in DEPARTMENT ✓. - `Bob → 20`: 20 exists in DEPARTMENT ✓. - `Carol → 99`: 99 does NOT exist in DEPARTMENT → **violation**. ??? success "**Conclusion.**" `Carol`'s `dept_id = 99` is a dangling reference. The DBMS would reject this tuple (unless `dept_id` were NULL).

docs.title: 2.13 — Why the Relational Model Dominates
docs.text: Six reasons Reason Explanation Simple One data structure: the relation Mathematically grounded Set theory + first-order logic Query algebra Provably equivalent to relational calculus Data independence Physical storage is hidden Standardized SQL (Chapter 6) Implementable Efficient storage and indexing (Chapter 7)   !!! tip "The historical argument"     Codd's 1970 paper was a **manifesto**: it argued that a simple data model with a formal algebra could replace the tangled hierarchical and network models. Fifty years later, it has won.

docs.title: Chapter 2 — key takeaways
docs.text: **1.** Three categories of data model: **conceptual** (ER), **logical** (relational), **physical** (files).     **2.** A **relation** is a set of tuples over a schema; each attribute takes values from a **domain**.     **3.** Four key levels: **superkey**, **candidate key**, **primary key**, **foreign key**. Every candidate is a superkey, but not vice versa.     **4.** **Entity-integrity:** primary keys are never NULL. **Referential-integrity:** foreign keys either are NULL or match a primary key.     **5.** **Referential actions** (RESTRICT, CASCADE, SET NULL, SET DEFAULT) determine what happens on delete/update of the referenced key.     **6.** **Schema** vs **instance** — structure vs. current data. The schema changes rarely; the instance constantly.

docs.title: Next — Chapter 3
docs.text:
Conceptual Design and E-R Modelling.

- The three design phases. - **Entities**, **attributes**, **relationships**. - **Cardinality ratios** and **participation constraints**. - **Weak entities** and identifying relationships. - **EER concepts:** subclasses, specialisation, generalisation, categories. - The **COMPANY** case study. Chapter 2 described the target model. Chapter 3 describes how to **design** a database from requirements — before writing a single line of SQL.

docs.title: Chapter 3 — Conceptual Design and E-R Modelling
Learning outcomes
docs.text: 1. Describe the **three phases of database design** and where conceptual design fits.     2. Draw ER diagrams with **entities**, **attributes**, **relationships**, **cardinality ratios**, and **participation constraints**.     3. Model **weak entities** with identifying relationships and partial keys.     4. Apply **EER concepts**: subclasses, superclasses, specialisation, generalisation, categories.     5. Build a complete ER diagram for the **COMPANY** database.

docs.title: 3.1 — The Three Design Phases
docs.text: Elmasri §3.1 Phase Input Output Conceptual design Requirements ER / EER model Logical design Conceptual model Relational schema Physical design Logical schema File structures, indexes   !!! tip "Why conceptual design matters most"     Errors in conceptual design **propagate everywhere**. A wrong entity or relationship cannot be fixed in later phases without redesigning. Conceptual design is also the phase where **communication with users** happens.     ???+ warning "Conceptual design is DBMS-independent"     The conceptual model must **not** mention tables, indexes, or SQL. Those belong to later phases. The ER model describes **what data means**, not how it will be stored.

docs.title: 3.2 — The ER Model Components
docs.text: Three building blocks Component Purpose Example Entity type A category of distinguishable things EMPLOYEE, PROJECT Attribute A property of an entity type name, salary Relationship type An association between two entity types WORKS_FOR, MANAGES ???+ info "Instance vs type" - **Entity type** — the category (`EMPLOYEE`). - **Entity** — an individual (`Alice`). - **Relationship type** — the association (`WORKS_FOR`). - **Relationship instance** — one specific link (`Alice WORKS_FOR Sales`).

docs.title: 3.3 — Attribute Types
docs.text: Six kinds of attributes Type Definition Notation Simple Single atomic value Ellipse Composite Composed of sub-attributes Ellipse with sub-ellipses Multivalued Multiple values per entity Double ellipse Derived Computed from other attributes Dashed ellipse Key Uniquely identifies Underlined Partial key Identifies within an owner's set (weak entities) Dashed underline   ???+ info "Examples"     - `address` — composite (street, city, zip).     - `phone` — multivalued (a person has many).     - `age` — derived (from `birth_date`).     - `ssn` — key.     - `dep_name` — partial key of a weak `DEPENDENT`.     !!! tip "When to model a multivalued attribute vs. a new entity"     If the values are **simple** (a phone number, a city), use a multivalued attribute. If they have their **own attributes** (a university degree with `year`, `major`, `GPA`), create a separate entity type. Attribute = "property of", entity = "independent existence".

docs.title: 3.4 — Entity and Relationship Notation
docs.text: Standard ER diagram notation Symbol Meaning Rectangle Entity type Double rectangle Weak entity type Ellipse Attribute Underlined attribute Key Dashed ellipse Derived attribute Double ellipse Multivalued attribute Diamond Relationship type Double diamond Identifying relationship (weak) Line Participation link Double line Total participation Label 1, N, M Cardinality ratio

docs.title: 3.5 — Cardinality Ratios
docs.text:
Three ratios

For a relationship between entity types \(A\) and \(B\):

Ratio Meaning 1:1 One \(A\) relates to at most one \(B\), and vice versa 1:N One \(A\) relates to many \(B\), but each \(B\) relates to one \(A\) M:N Many \(A\) relate to many \(B\) ???+ info "Real-world examples" - **1:1** — `DEPARTMENT` `MANAGES` `EMPLOYEE` (one dept has one manager; one manager manages one dept). - **1:N** — `DEPARTMENT` `CONTROLS` `PROJECT` (one dept controls many projects; each project belongs to one dept). - **M:N** — `EMPLOYEE` `WORKS_ON` `PROJECT` (an employee works on many projects; a project has many employees). !!! warning "Cardinality is about the association, not the entities" The 1:N in `DEPARTMENT CONTROLS PROJECT` means *one dept controls many projects*. It does not say "a project has many employees" — that's a different relationship.

docs.title: 3.6 — Participation Constraints
docs.text:
Total vs partial
  • Total participation (double line) — every entity of the type must participate.
  • Partial participation (single line) — some entities may not participate.
???+ info "Examples in COMPANY" | Relationship | Participation | |---|---| | `EMPLOYEE WORKS_FOR DEPARTMENT` | **Total** on EMPLOYEE (every employee works for a department) | | `EMPLOYEE MANAGES DEPARTMENT` | **Partial** on EMPLOYEE (not every employee manages) | | `PROJECT CONTROLLED_BY DEPARTMENT` | **Total** on PROJECT (every project belongs to a department) | !!! tip "Participation determines NOT NULL in the schema" Total participation on the "N" side becomes **NOT NULL** in the relational schema (Chapter 4). Partial participation allows NULL.

docs.title: Worked example 3.1 — A simple ER diagram
docs.text:
Problem:

Model a small library: - Books have an ISBN, title, and year. - Members have a member_id and name. - A member can borrow books; each loan records the borrow date.

???+ note "**Step 1 — identify entities.**" - `BOOK` (ISBN, title, year). - `MEMBER` (member_id, name). - `LOAN` — records a borrowing event. ??? info "**Step 2 — decide: entity or relationship?**" `LOAN` could be a **relationship** (BOOK-MEMBER) with attribute `borrow_date`. But if we want to track multiple loans over time, `LOAN` should be an **entity**. ??? info "**Step 3 — relationships.**" - `BOOK` — `LOAN` — `MEMBER` with cardinality 1:N and M:1 (a book can be loaned many times; a member can borrow many times). ??? success "**Step 4 — the diagram.**" 
MEMBER(1) ──< LOAN >── (1)BOOK
              |
           borrow_date
Actually, the correct model is: MEMBER 1 — N LOAN, BOOK 1 — N LOAN. Each loan ties one book to one member.

docs.title: 3.7 — Weak Entities
docs.text:
Definition (Elmasri §3.5)

A weak entity type has no key attribute of its own and depends on an owner entity type through an identifying relationship.

???+ info "Key characteristics" - **No key of its own.** - Has a **partial key** — an attribute that is unique only within one owner's set. - The full key = (owner's key, partial key). - Shown as a **double rectangle** with a **double diamond** identifying relationship. ???+ note "Example: `DEPENDENT`" - `DEPENDENT` (of an `EMPLOYEE`) has `dep_name`, `sex`, `birth_date`, `relationship`. - `dep_name` is unique only **within one employee**. - Full key: `(essn, dep_name)`. - Cannot exist without an employee.

docs.title: Worked example 3.2 — Model with a weak entity
docs.text:
Problem:

A company has departments. Each department has projects. Each project has parts. A part is identified by a part_number that is unique only within its project.

???+ note "**Step 1 — regular entities.**" `DEPARTMENT(dnumber, dname)`, `PROJECT(pnumber, pname)`. ??? info "**Step 2 — the weak entity.**" `PART(part_number, name, weight)` — `part_number` unique only within a project. ??? info "**Step 3 — identifying relationship.**" `PART` **has** `PROJECT` (double diamond). Full key of `PART` = `(pnumber, part_number)`. ??? success "**Step 4 — the diagram.**" 
DEPARTMENT(1) ──< PROJECT >── 1
                    ||||
                    └────< PART > (weak, partial key: part_number)

docs.title: 3.8 — EER Concepts: Overview
docs.text: Enhanced ER adds four constructs Construct Purpose Subclass / Superclass Classification hierarchy Specialisation Top-down decomposition Generalisation Bottom-up combination Category (Union) Entity belongs to one of several superclasses   ???+ info "Why EER?"     The basic ER model cannot express **is-a** relationships elegantly. EER adds inheritance — subclasses inherit the superclass's attributes and relationships.

docs.title: 3.9 — Subclass and Superclass
docs.text:
Definition

A subclass is a subset of a superclass's entities. Each subclass member is also a superclass member (is-a relationship).

???+ info "Example" - `EMPLOYEE` is the superclass. - `SECRETARY`, `ENGINEER`, `TECHNICIAN` are subclasses. - Every engineer **is an** employee; not every employee is an engineer. ???+ note "Attribute inheritance" Subclasses inherit **all** attributes and relationship participations of their superclass — including inherited keys. !!! tip "When to model a subclass" Use a subclass when: - It has **its own attributes** (e.g., `ENGINEER` has `engineering_field`). - It has **its own relationships** (e.g., `ENGINEER` belongs to a `PROFESSIONAL_UNION`). - It has **its own participation** in a shared relationship.

docs.title: 3.10 — Specialisation and Generalisation
docs.text: Two directions, same diagram Process Direction Starting point Specialisation Top-down Start with one entity, identify subclasses Generalisation Bottom-up Start with several entities, combine into superclass   ???+ info "Example: specialisation"     Start with `EMPLOYEE`. Specialise into `SECRETARY`, `ENGINEER`, `TECHNICIAN` based on job function.     ???+ info "Example: generalisation"     Start with `CAR` and `TRUCK`. Generalise into `VEHICLE` (they share `price`, `max_speed`, `registration`).     !!! tip "The diagram is the same"     Both produce a superclass with a circle (or triangle) connecting to subclasses. Only the **direction of reasoning** differs — which affects the modelling conversation, not the notation.

docs.title: 3.11 — Constraints on Specialisation
docs.text: Two dimensions Dimension Values Meaning Disjointness Disjoint (d) An entity belongs to at most one subclass Overlapping (o) An entity may belong to multiple subclasses Completeness Total (double line) Every superclass entity belongs to some subclass Partial (single line) Some superclass entities belong to no subclass   ???+ info "The four combinations"     | Disjoint | Complete | Example |     |---|---|---|     | **D, Total** | every employee is exactly one of secretary/engineer/technician |     | **D, Partial** | some employees are unclassified |     | **O, Total** | every employee is at least one of manager/engineer (some are both) |     | **O, Partial** | some employees are neither manager nor engineer |     !!! warning "Common mistake"     Disjointness is a **constraint of the model**, not a claim about the world. If an employee can be both an engineer and a manager, the specialisation must be **overlapping**.

docs.title: Worked example 3.3 — EER for a university
docs.text:
Problem:

Model: - PERSON(pid, name, address). - A person can be a STUDENT (with major) and/or a FACULTY (with rank). - A STUDENT can be GRAD_STUDENT (with thesis_title) or UNDERGRAD_STUDENT (with year).

???+ note "**Step 1 — superclass.**" `PERSON`. ??? info "**Step 2 — first-level specialisation.**" `STUDENT` and `FACULTY`. **Overlapping**, **partial** — a person may be neither, and may be both. ??? info "**Step 3 — second-level specialisation.**" `GRAD_STUDENT` and `UNDERGRAD_STUDENT` under `STUDENT`. **Disjoint**, **total** — a student is exactly one. ??? success "**Step 4 — the diagram.**" 
              PERSON
               /  \
          STUDENT  FACULTY
             / \   (overlapping, partial)
            /   \
   GRAD_STUDENT  UNDERGRAD_STUDENT
   (disjoint, total)
Walk through why the first-level specialisation must be overlapping: a graduate teaching assistant is both a student and faculty. If we marked it disjoint, the model would forbid this common case. This is a favourite exam question — the disjoint/total choices must be justified from the requirements, not assumed.

docs.title: 3.12 — Categories (Union Types)
docs.text:
Definition

A category (or union type) combines entities from disjoint superclasses. An entity belongs to exactly one of the superclasses.

???+ info "Example" An `OWNER` may be a `PERSON`, a `BANK`, or a `COMPANY` — **mutually exclusive** alternatives. 
PERSON    BANK    COMPANY
   \       |       /
    \      |      /
     \     |     /
      ◯ ∪ ◯
        |
      OWNER
???+ info "Category vs specialisation" | Aspect | Category (union) | Specialisation | |---|---|---| | Direction | Subclass → multiple superclasses | Superclass → subclasses | | Mutually exclusive? | **Yes** | Depends on disjoint/overlapping | | Member of one superclass? | **Yes, exactly one** | No |

docs.title: Worked example 3.4 — Category in a vehicle registration system
docs.text:
Problem:

Vehicles can be registered. Owners can be: - Individuals (PERSON). - Companies (COMPANY). - Government agencies (GOV_AGENCY).

Each owner is exactly one of these — never a combination.

???+ note "**Step 1 — why category, not specialisation?**" Because a `PERSON`, a `COMPANY`, and a `GOV_AGENCY` are **disjoint** types — an entity cannot be a person and a company at the same time. Specialisation would imply a common superclass; here there is no natural common superclass, only a union. ??? info "**Step 2 — the diagram.**" 
PERSON    COMPANY    GOV_AGENCY
   \          |          /
    \         |         /
     ◯─────∪─────◯
          |
        OWNER  (has category membership)
          |
      REGISTERED_VEHICLE
??? success "**Step 3 — the rule.**" Each `OWNER` is a member of **exactly one** of the three superclasses. The category declares "these three are alternatives for the role of owner".

docs.title: 3.13 — The COMPANY Case Study
docs.text:
Requirements
  • Departments have a unique name, a number, and one employee who manages them.
  • Each department controls several projects, each with a unique name, number, and single location.
  • Employees have a name, SSN, sex, address, salary, birth date, and belong to a department.
  • Employees may work on several projects (hours per week).
  • Employees may have dependents (name, sex, birth date, relationship).

docs.title: Worked example 3.5 — COMPANY ER diagram
docs.text:
Problem:

Draw the complete ER diagram for COMPANY.

???+ note "**Step 1 — entities.**" `EMPLOYEE`, `DEPARTMENT`, `PROJECT`, `DEPENDENT` (weak). ??? info "**Step 2 — relationships.**" - `EMPLOYEE WORKS_FOR DEPARTMENT` (N:1, total on EMPLOYEE). - `EMPLOYEE MANAGES DEPARTMENT` (1:1, partial on both). - `DEPARTMENT CONTROLS PROJECT` (1:N, total on PROJECT). - `EMPLOYEE WORKS_ON PROJECT` (M:N, with `hours`). - `EMPLOYEE DEPENDENT_OF DEPENDENT` (1:N, identifying). - `EMPLOYEE SUPERVISES EMPLOYEE` (1:N, recursive). ??? info "**Step 3 — attributes.**" - `DEPARTMENT`: `dnumber` (key), `dname` (unique), `locations` (multivalued). - `PROJECT`: `pnumber` (key), `pname`, `location`. - `EMPLOYEE`: `ssn` (key), `name` (composite: first, middle, last), `sex`, `address`, `salary`, `bdate`. - `DEPENDENT`: `dep_name` (partial key), `sex`, `bdate`, `relationship`. ??? success "**Step 4 — cardinalities and participation.**" | Relationship | Ratio | Participation | |---|---|---| | `WORKS_FOR` | N:1 | Total on EMPLOYEE | | `MANAGES` | 1:1 | Partial on both | | `CONTROLS` | 1:N | Total on PROJECT | | `WORKS_ON` | M:N | Partial on both | | `DEPENDENT_OF` | 1:N | Total on DEPENDENT |

docs.title: 3.14 — COMPANY EER Extension
docs.text:
Specialisation of EMPLOYEE

Three subclasses based on job function: - SECRETARY — with typing_speed. - ENGINEER — with engineering_field. - TECHNICIAN — with skill_level.

???+ info "Constraints" - **Disjoint** — a secretary is not an engineer. - **Total** — every employee is one of the three (in this simplified model). ???+ note "Second specialisation" `HOURLY_EMPLOYEE` and `SALARIED_EMPLOYEE` (disjoint, total). !!! tip "Multiple specialisations" An entity type can be specialised in **more than one way** — `EMPLOYEE` can be (a) secretary/engineer/technician and (b) hourly/salaried. These are independent dimensions.

docs.title: 3.15 — Common Modelling Pitfalls
docs.text:
Pitfall 1 — modelling a relationship as an entity

MARRIAGE between two PERSONs has its own attributes (date, location). Model it as an entity with two relationships to PERSON, not as a plain relationship.

??? warning "Pitfall 2 — entity with only one attribute as key" A `PHONE(phone_number)` with only `phone_number` as attribute is really an attribute of `PERSON` (multivalued). Don't create entities without their own meaningful attributes. ??? warning "Pitfall 3 — modelling time as a relationship" If "who was manager when" matters, model `MANAGEMENT(employee, department, start_date, end_date)` as an **entity** — a relationship has no notion of time. ??? warning "Pitfall 4 — confusing subclass and category" Subclass = **is-a** (every engineer is an employee). Category = **is one of** (a vehicle owner is a person OR a company, not both).

docs.title: Chapter 3 — key takeaways
docs.text: **1.** Conceptual design comes first and errors here propagate. The conceptual model is DBMS-independent.     **2.** Three building blocks: **entities**, **attributes** (simple, composite, multivalued, derived, key), **relationships**.     **3.** **Cardinality ratios** (1:1, 1:N, M:N) and **participation** (total, partial) fully specify a relationship.     **4.** **Weak entities** have no key of their own; their key = (owner's key, partial key).     **5.** **EER** adds subclass/superclass, specialisation/generalisation, and categories — with **disjoint/overlapping** and **total/partial** constraints.     **6.** Model entities — not relationships — when the "relationship" has its own attributes or changes over time.

docs.title: Next — Chapter 4
docs.text:
Logical Design and Normalisation.

- The 7-step **ER-to-relational mapping**. - The 2 extra steps for EER constructs. - **Functional dependencies** and **Armstrong's axioms**. - Closure, minimal cover. - **Normal forms 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF**. Chapter 3 gave a beautiful conceptual model. Chapter 4 turns it into **tables** — and proves that the tables are well-designed.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text: 1. Apply the **7-step ER-to-relational mapping** to any ER diagram.     2. Apply the **2 extra steps** for EER constructs (specialisation, categories).     3. Compute **closures** and **minimal covers** for sets of functional dependencies.     4. Determine whether a schema is in **1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF**.     5. Decompose a schema into 3NF or BCNF while preserving properties.

docs.title: 4.1 — ER-to-Relational Mapping Overview
docs.text: The 7 steps (Elmasri §9.1) Step Maps 1 Regular entity types 2 Weak entity types 3 Binary 1:1 relationships 4 Binary 1:N relationships 5 Binary M:N relationships 6 Multivalued attributes 7 N-ary relationships   !!! tip "The order matters"     Steps 1–2 handle entities and their attributes. Steps 3–5 handle relationships. Steps 6–7 handle the "extras". Following the order avoids duplicate table creation.

docs.title: 4.2 — Step 1: Regular Entity Types
docs.text:
Rule

Each regular entity becomes a relation: - Include all simple attributes. - For each composite attribute, include only its simple components. - Choose one key attribute as the primary key.

???+ info "Example: `EMPLOYEE(ssn, name(first, middle, last), sex, address, salary, bdate)`" Becomes: 
CREATE TABLE EMPLOYEE (
    ssn     CHAR(9) PRIMARY KEY,
    first_name VARCHAR(30),
    middle_name VARCHAR(30),
    last_name   VARCHAR(30),
    sex     CHAR(1),
    address VARCHAR(100),
    salary  DECIMAL(10,2),
    bdate   DATE
);
!!! warning "Don't create a table for the composite attribute" `name` is composite, but it is **not** a separate table. Its **simple components** (`first_name`, `middle_name`, `last_name`) become columns of `EMPLOYEE`.

docs.title: 4.3 — Step 2: Weak Entity Types
docs.text:
Rule

Each weak entity becomes a relation with: - Its own attributes. - The owner's primary key as a foreign key. - Primary key = (owner's primary key, partial key).

???+ info "Example: `DEPENDENT`" 
CREATE TABLE DEPENDENT (
    essn            CHAR(9),
    dependent_name  VARCHAR(50),
    sex             CHAR(1),
    birth_date      DATE,
    relationship    VARCHAR(20),
    PRIMARY KEY (essn, dependent_name),
    FOREIGN KEY (essn) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(ssn)
);
!!! tip "The full key is composite" `dependent_name` is a **partial key** — unique only within one employee. The full key must include `essn` to be globally unique.

docs.title: 4.4 — Step 3: Binary 1:1 Relationships
docs.text:
Rule

Put the primary key of one side as a foreign key in the other side.

Prefer the side with total participation — that ensures every tuple on that side has a non-NULL reference.

???+ info "Example: `EMPLOYEE MANAGES DEPARTMENT` (1:1)" Both sides are partial in the COMPANY model. Standard choice: put the foreign key in `DEPARTMENT`: 
ALTER TABLE DEPARTMENT
    ADD COLUMN mgr_ssn CHAR(9),
    ADD FOREIGN KEY (mgr_ssn) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(ssn);
!!! warning "Why NOT in EMPLOYEE?" If `mgr_dno` were in `EMPLOYEE`, most employees would have NULL there (only one manager per department). Putting the reference in `DEPARTMENT` is more natural. ???+ note "The cross-reference option" An alternative is a **cross-reference table** with both foreign keys. This is used when neither side has total participation and the relationship has its own attributes.

docs.title: 4.5 — Step 4: Binary 1:N Relationships
4.6 — Step 5: Binary M:N Relationships
docs.text:
Rule

Create a new relation with: - The primary keys of both sides as foreign keys. - Any relationship attributes (e.g., hours). - Primary key = the combination of both foreign keys.

???+ info "Example: `EMPLOYEE WORKS_ON PROJECT` (M:N with `hours`)" 
CREATE TABLE WORKS_ON (
    essn  CHAR(9),
    pno   INT,
    hours DECIMAL(3,1),
    PRIMARY KEY (essn, pno),
    FOREIGN KEY (essn) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(ssn),
    FOREIGN KEY (pno)  REFERENCES PROJECT(pnumber)
);
!!! warning "M:N cannot be a foreign key on either side" A single `EMPLOYEE.ssn` cannot reference many projects, and a single `PROJECT.pnumber` cannot reference many employees. The cross-reference table is **required**.

docs.title: 4.7 — Step 6: Multivalued Attributes
docs.text:
Rule

Create a new relation with: - The multivalued attribute itself. - The owner's primary key as a foreign key. - Primary key = (owner's primary key, attribute).

???+ info "Example: `DEPARTMENT.locations` (multivalued)" 
CREATE TABLE DEPT_LOCATIONS (
    dnumber   INT,
    dlocation VARCHAR(50),
    PRIMARY KEY (dnumber, dlocation),
    FOREIGN KEY (dnumber) REFERENCES DEPARTMENT(dnumber)
);
!!! tip "Why not keep it in DEPARTMENT?" A relational attribute must be **atomic** (1NF). A multivalued attribute would violate 1NF. The separate table is the standard fix.

docs.title: 4.8 — Step 7: N-ary Relationships
docs.text:
Rule

Create a new relation with: - The primary keys of all participating entities as foreign keys. - Any relationship attributes. - Primary key = the combination of all foreign keys (or a subset if some participants are functionally determined).

???+ info "Example: `SUPPLIES(supplier, project, part, quantity)`" 
CREATE TABLE SUPPLIES (
    supplier_id INT,
    project_id  INT,
    part_id     INT,
    quantity    INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (supplier_id, project_id, part_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (supplier_id) REFERENCES SUPPLIER(supplier_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (project_id)  REFERENCES PROJECT(project_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (part_id)     REFERENCES PART(part_id)
);
!!! warning "Ternary ≠ three binary relationships" A ternary `SUPPLIES` means "supplier supplies part **to** project" — a joint constraint. Three separate binary relationships would lose the joint semantics.

docs.title: Worked example 4.1 — Map the COMPANY database
docs.text:
Problem:

Map the COMPANY ER model from Chapter 3 to a relational schema.

???+ note "**Step 1 — regular entities.**" 
CREATE TABLE EMPLOYEE (
    ssn CHAR(9) PRIMARY KEY,
    first_name VARCHAR(30), middle_name VARCHAR(30), last_name VARCHAR(30),
    sex CHAR(1), address VARCHAR(100), salary DECIMAL(10,2), bdate DATE
);
CREATE TABLE DEPARTMENT (
    dnumber INT PRIMARY KEY,
    dname VARCHAR(50) UNIQUE
);
CREATE TABLE PROJECT (
    pnumber INT PRIMARY KEY,
    pname VARCHAR(50), location VARCHAR(50)
);
??? info "**Step 2 — weak entity.**" 
CREATE TABLE DEPENDENT (
    essn CHAR(9),
    dependent_name VARCHAR(50),
    sex CHAR(1), birth_date DATE, relationship VARCHAR(20),
    PRIMARY KEY (essn, dependent_name),
    FOREIGN KEY (essn) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(ssn)
);
??? info "**Step 3 — 1:1 `MANAGES`.**" 
ALTER TABLE DEPARTMENT ADD COLUMN mgr_ssn CHAR(9),
    ADD FOREIGN KEY (mgr_ssn) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(ssn);
??? info "**Step 4 — 1:N `WORKS_FOR`, `CONTROLS`, `SUPERVISES`.**" 
ALTER TABLE EMPLOYEE ADD COLUMN dno INT,
    ADD FOREIGN KEY (dno) REFERENCES DEPARTMENT(dnumber);
ALTER TABLE EMPLOYEE ADD COLUMN super_ssn CHAR(9),
    ADD FOREIGN KEY (super_ssn) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(ssn);
ALTER TABLE PROJECT ADD COLUMN dnum INT,
    ADD FOREIGN KEY (dnum) REFERENCES DEPARTMENT(dnumber);
??? info "**Step 5 — M:N `WORKS_ON`.**" 
CREATE TABLE WORKS_ON (
    essn CHAR(9), pno INT, hours DECIMAL(3,1),
    PRIMARY KEY (essn, pno),
    FOREIGN KEY (essn) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(ssn),
    FOREIGN KEY (pno)  REFERENCES PROJECT(pnumber)
);
??? info "**Step 6 — multivalued `locations`.**" 
CREATE TABLE DEPT_LOCATIONS (
    dnumber INT, dlocation VARCHAR(50),
    PRIMARY KEY (dnumber, dlocation),
    FOREIGN KEY (dnumber) REFERENCES DEPARTMENT(dnumber)
);
??? success "**Result.**" Seven tables: `EMPLOYEE`, `DEPARTMENT`, `PROJECT`, `DEPENDENT`, `WORKS_ON`, `DEPT_LOCATIONS`. All keys and foreign keys defined. No redundancy.

docs.title: 4.9 — EER Extra Steps
docs.text:
Step 8 — Specialisation / Generalisation

Four options (Elmasri §9.2):

Option Structure When to use 8A Superclass table + subclass tables (each references superclass) Any specialisation 8B Subclass tables only (each contains all superclass attributes) Total, disjoint specialisation 8C Single table + type discriminator Disjoint, no subclass-specific attributes 8D Single table + multiple boolean type attributes Overlapping ???+ note "Step 9 — Categories (Union types)" Create one relation per subclass, plus a **category table** that holds the primary key of each participant and a **type discriminator**. The category table's rows reference the appropriate subclass tables.

docs.title: Worked example 4.2 — Map EER specialisation (8A vs 8C)
docs.text:
Problem:

EMPLOYEE has subclasses SECRETARY(typing_speed) and ENGINEER(engineering_field). Specialisation is disjoint, total. Map it two ways.

???+ note "**Option 8A — separate tables.**" 
CREATE TABLE EMPLOYEE (
    ssn CHAR(9) PRIMARY KEY, first_name VARCHAR(30), last_name VARCHAR(30),
    salary DECIMAL(10,2), dno INT
);
CREATE TABLE SECRETARY (
    ssn CHAR(9) PRIMARY KEY,
    typing_speed INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (ssn) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(ssn)
);
CREATE TABLE ENGINEER (
    ssn CHAR(9) PRIMARY KEY,
    engineering_field VARCHAR(50),
    FOREIGN KEY (ssn) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(ssn)
);
Every employee query must `JOIN` with the subclass table. ??? info "**Option 8C — single table with discriminator.**" 
CREATE TABLE EMPLOYEE (
    ssn CHAR(9) PRIMARY KEY, first_name VARCHAR(30), last_name VARCHAR(30),
    salary DECIMAL(10,2), dno INT,
    emp_type CHAR(1) CHECK (emp_type IN ('S','E')),
    typing_speed INT,
    engineering_field VARCHAR(50)
);
Subclass-specific attributes are NULL for the "wrong" type. **Simpler** queries but **NULLs** everywhere. ??? success "**Which to choose?**" - **8A** when there are **many** subclass-specific attributes and queries usually touch subclasses separately. - **8C** when subclass-specific attributes are **few** and queries usually join back to the superclass.

docs.title: 4.10 — Functional Dependencies (FDs)
docs.text:
Definition (Elmasri §14.2)

A functional dependency \(X \to Y\) on relation \(R\) holds if, for every two tuples \(t_1, t_2\) of \(R\):

\[ t_1[X] = t_2[X] \implies t_1[Y] = t_2[Y]. \]

In words: \(X\) determines \(Y\) — the value of \(X\) uniquely determines the value of \(Y\).

???+ info "Example" - `ssn → name` — two employees with the same SSN have the same name. - `ssn → (name, bdate, address)` — an SSN determines the whole employee record. - `(ssn, pno) → hours` — the hours on a project depend on both the employee and the project. !!! warning "The direction is one-way" `X → Y` **does not** imply `Y → X`. `ssn → name` holds, but `name → ssn` does not (two employees can share a name).

docs.title: 4.11 — Armstrong's Axioms
docs.text:
Three inference rules (sound and complete)

Reflexivity. If \(Y \subseteq X\), then \(X \to Y\).

Augmentation. If \(X \to Y\), then \(XZ \to YZ\) for any \(Z\).

Transitivity. If \(X \to Y\) and \(Y \to Z\), then \(X \to Z\).

???+ info "Derived rules" - **Union:** $X \to Y$ and $X \to Z$ ⇒ $X \to YZ$. - **Decomposition:** $X \to YZ$ ⇒ $X \to Y$ and $X \to Z$. - **Pseudotransitivity:** $X \to Y$ and $WY \to Z$ ⇒ $WX \to Z$. !!! tip "Sound and complete" **Sound** = every derived FD is true in every instance satisfying the original FDs. **Complete** = every FD implied by the originals can be derived. Armstrong's axioms are both.

docs.title: 4.12 — Closure of Attribute Sets
docs.text:
Definition

The closure \(X^+\) of an attribute set \(X\) under \(F\) is the set of all attributes functionally determined by \(X\) using Armstrong's axioms.

???+ info "Algorithm" 
X+ := X
repeat:
    for each FD (A → B) in F:
        if A ⊆ X+ and B ⊄ X+:
            X+ := X+ ∪ B
until X+ does not change
???+ success "Uses of closure" - **Test if $X$ is a superkey:** $X^+$ = all attributes. - **Test if $X \to Y$ holds:** $Y \subseteq X^+$. - **Compute candidate keys:** find minimal $X$ with $X^+$ = all attributes.

docs.title: Worked example 4.3 — Compute \((AB)^+\)
docs.text:
Problem:

\(R(A,B,C,D,E)\) with \(F = \{AB \to C,\ C \to D,\ D \to E\}\). Compute \((AB)^+\).

???+ note "**Step 1 — initialise.**" $(AB)^+ = \{A, B\}$. ??? info "**Step 2 — apply FDs.**" - $AB \to C$: $AB \subseteq (AB)^+$, so add $C$ → $\{A,B,C\}$. - $C \to D$: $C \subseteq (AB)^+$, so add $D$ → $\{A,B,C,D\}$. - $D \to E$: $D \subseteq (AB)^+$, so add $E$ → $\{A,B,C,D,E\}$. ??? success "**Result.**" $(AB)^+ = \{A, B, C, D, E\}$ — all attributes. So $AB$ is a **superkey**. **Is $AB$ a candidate key?** Check $(A)^+ = \{A\}$, $(B)^+ = \{B\}$ — neither. So $AB$ is a **candidate key** (minimal).

docs.title: 4.13 — Minimal Cover
docs.text:
Definition

A minimal cover \(F_{\min}\) of \(F\) is a set of FDs equivalent to \(F\) such that:

  1. Every FD has a single attribute on the right.
  2. No redundant FD — removing any loses equivalence.
  3. No redundant attribute on the left — the left side is minimal.
???+ info "Algorithm" 1. Decompose RHS: $X \to AB$ becomes $X \to A$, $X \to B$. 2. Remove redundant LHS attributes: if $A$ is redundant in $AB \to C$ (i.e., $B \to C$ after removing $A$), drop $A$. 3. Remove redundant FDs: for each FD, remove it and see if it's still implied. !!! tip "Minimal covers are not unique" Different removal orders give different but equivalent minimal covers. Any is valid.

docs.title: Worked example 4.4 — Compute a minimal cover
docs.text:
Problem:

\(F = \{A \to B, ABCD \to E, EF \to G, EF \to H, ACDF \to EG\}\). Compute a minimal cover.

???+ note "**Step 1 — decompose RHS.**" - $A \to B$ - $ABCD \to E$ - $EF \to G$, $EF \to H$ - $ACDF \to E$, $ACDF \to G$ ??? info "**Step 2 — remove redundant LHS attributes.**" - For $ABCD \to E$: is $B, C, D$ redundant? Compute $(ACD)^+$. $A \to B$, so $(ACD)^+ \supseteq ABCD \to E$. So $B$ is redundant. New FD: $ACD \to E$. - Similarly, $C$ and $D$ may be reducible further; compute $(AD)^+ \supseteq E$? Check step by step. ??? info "**Step 3 — remove redundant FDs.**" Test each FD by removing it and checking if the remainder implies it via closure. ??? success "**Result.**" A possible minimal cover: $\{A \to B, A \to E, A \to G, EF \to H\}$ (depending on redundancy analysis). The exact form varies, but the closure is preserved.

docs.title: 4.14 — Normal Forms Overview
docs.text: The four normal forms Normal Form Removes Requires 1NF Multivalued attributes Atomic values 2NF Partial dependencies 1NF + no partial dependency on part of a key 3NF Transitive dependencies 2NF + every FD has superkey LHS or prime RHS BCNF All non-superkey determinants 3NF + every FD has superkey LHS   !!! tip "The hierarchy"     BCNF $\subset$ 3NF $\subset$ 2NF $\subset$ 1NF. Every BCNF relation is 3NF, every 3NF is 2NF, every 2NF is 1NF.

docs.title: 4.15 — 1NF — First Normal Form
docs.text:
1NF (Elmasri §14.3)

A relation is in 1NF if every attribute value is atomic — no sets, no lists, no nested relations.

???+ info "Violation example" 
STUDENT(student_id, name, phones)
101, Alice, {555-1234, 555-5678}      ← multivalued
Fix: separate table `STUDENT_PHONE(student_id, phone)`. !!! warning "1NF is not optional" Relational algebra and SQL assume atomic values. Without 1NF, projection, join, and aggregate become ill-defined.

docs.title: 4.16 — 2NF — Second Normal Form
docs.text:
2NF

A relation is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on every candidate key.

???+ info "What is a partial dependency?" A **partial dependency** exists when a non-prime attribute depends on **part** of a composite candidate key, not the whole key. Example: `WORKS_ON(essn, pno, hours, ename)` with FD `essn → ename`. `ename` depends only on `essn`, part of the composite key `(essn, pno)`. **Violates 2NF.** ???+ info "Fix" Decompose so that every non-prime attribute depends on the full key: 
EMPLOYEE(ssn, ename, ...)
WORKS_ON(essn, pno, hours)
!!! tip "2NF only matters for composite keys" If a relation has a single-attribute primary key, it is **automatically in 2NF** — no partial dependency is possible.

docs.title: 4.17 — 3NF — Third Normal Form
docs.text:
3NF (Elmasri §14.4)

A relation is in 3NF if it is in 2NF and no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on any candidate key.

Equivalently: for every non-trivial FD \(X \to Y\):

  • \(X\) is a superkey, or
  • \(Y\) is a prime attribute (part of some candidate key).
???+ info "What is a transitive dependency?" `X → Y → Z` where `X` is a key and `Z` is non-prime. `Z` depends on `X` only through `Y`. Example: `EMPLOYEE(ssn, name, dno, dname)`. `ssn → dno` (key → non-key) and `dno → dname` (non-key → non-key). `dname` is transitively dependent on `ssn`. **Violates 3NF.** ???+ info "Fix" Decompose into `EMPLOYEE(ssn, name, dno)` and `DEPARTMENT(dno, dname)`.

docs.title: 4.18 — BCNF — Boyce-Codd Normal Form
docs.text:
BCNF

A relation is in BCNF if, for every non-trivial FD \(X \to Y\):

\(X\) is a superkey.

(No exception for prime attributes.)

???+ info "BCNF is stricter than 3NF" 3NF allows $Y$ prime even when $X$ is not superkey. BCNF forbids this. Example: `R(A,B,C)` with `AB → C, C → B`. Candidate keys: `AB`, `AC`. `C → B` has non-superkey `C` but prime `B` → **3NF but not BCNF**. !!! warning "BCNF may lose dependency preservation" The classic 3NF-but-not-BCNF relation above cannot be BCNF-decomposed without losing the FD `AB → C`. So 3NF is the practical target when dependency preservation matters.

docs.title: Worked example 4.5 — Full normalisation
docs.text:
Problem:

EMP_PROJ(ssn, ename, pno, pname, hours)
FDs: ssn → ename, pno → pname, (ssn, pno) → hours. Normalise to 3NF.

???+ note "**Step 1 — candidate key.**" Only `(ssn, pno)` is a candidate key. Prime attributes: `ssn`, `pno`. Non-prime: `ename`, `pname`, `hours`. ??? info "**Step 2 — check 1NF.**" All values atomic. **Satisfied.** ??? info "**Step 3 — check 2NF.**" `ssn → ename`: partial dependency (ename on ssn only). `pno → pname`: partial dependency. **Violates 2NF.** ??? info "**Step 4 — decompose for 2NF.**" - `EMP(ssn, ename)` - `PROJ(pno, pname)` - `WORKS_ON(ssn, pno, hours)` ??? info "**Step 5 — check 3NF.**" - `EMP`: `ssn` is the key; `ssn → ename` OK. - `PROJ`: `pno` is the key; `pno → pname` OK. - `WORKS_ON`: `(ssn, pno)` is the key; `(ssn, pno) → hours` OK. No transitive dependencies. **All three are in 3NF (and in BCNF).** ??? success "**Result.**" `EMP(ssn, ename)`, `PROJ(pno, pname)`, `WORKS_ON(ssn, pno, hours)` — lossless, dependency-preserving, in BCNF.

docs.title: Worked example 4.6 — 3NF but not BCNF
docs.text:
Problem:

R(A, B, C) with FDs AB → C, C → B. Is it in 3NF? BCNF?

???+ note "**Step 1 — candidate keys.**" - $(AB)^+ = \{A, B, C\}$ → `AB` is a candidate key. - $(AC)^+ = \{A, C, B\}$ → `AC` is a candidate key. Prime attributes: `A, B, C`. Non-prime: none. ??? info "**Step 2 — check 3NF.**" For every FD $X \to Y$: $X$ superkey **or** $Y$ prime. - `AB → C`: `AB` is superkey. ✓ - `C → B`: `C` not superkey, but `B` is prime → satisfies 3NF. ✓ ??? info "**Step 3 — check BCNF.**" `C → B`: `C` is not a superkey. **Violates BCNF.** ??? success "**Conclusion.**" The relation is **3NF but not BCNF**. ???+ warning "BCNF decomposition loses dependency" Decompose into `R1(C, B)` and `R2(A, C)`. Lossless, BCNF. But `AB → C` now requires a **join** to verify — **dependency not preserved**.

docs.title: 4.19 — Decomposition Properties
docs.text: Two desirable properties Property Meaning Lossless join The natural join of the decomposed relations reconstructs the original exactly (no spurious tuples) Dependency preservation Every FD of the original is enforceable within a single decomposed relation   ???+ info "Testing for lossless join (binary decomposition)"     For $R$ decomposed into $R_1$ and $R_2$:      **Lossless iff** $R_1 \cap R_2 \to R_1$ **or** $R_1 \cap R_2 \to R_2$ holds.     ???+ info "The 3NF synthesis algorithm"     1. Compute a minimal cover $F_{\min}$.     2. For each FD $X \to A$ in $F_{\min}$, create a relation $XA$.     3. If no relation contains a candidate key of $R$, add one.      **Guarantees:** lossless, dependency-preserving, 3NF.     ???+ warning "BCNF decomposition is lossless but not dependency-preserving"     The classic 3NF-not-BCNF example shows that BCNF and dependency preservation can conflict. **3NF is the practical target** for OLTP systems.

docs.title: 4.20 — Informal Design Guidelines
docs.text:
Three guidelines (Elmasri §14.1)

1. Clear semantics. Each tuple should represent one entity or relationship, and each attribute should describe one property of that entity.

???+ note "2. No redundant information" Redundancy causes **update, insertion, and deletion anomalies**. The goal of normalization is to eliminate structural redundancy. ???+ note "3. Few NULLs" Excessive NULLs waste space and complicate joins, aggregates, and constraints. NULLs also indicate **ambiguous design**. !!! tip "Normalization is a design guideline, not a law" Sometimes denormalization is **deliberate** — data warehouses denormalize for query performance. But OLTP systems should normalize to 3NF (or BCNF when possible).

docs.title: Chapter 4 — key takeaways
docs.text: **1.** The **7-step ER-to-relational mapping** transforms any ER diagram into a relational schema. Order matters.     **2.** **EER specialisations** have four mapping options (8A–8D); **categories** use a type-discriminator table.     **3.** **Functional dependencies** $X \to Y$ mean $X$ determines $Y$. **Armstrong's axioms** (reflexivity, augmentation, transitivity) are sound and complete.     **4.** **Closure** $X^+$ tests whether $X$ is a superkey and whether $X \to Y$ holds. **Minimal cover** reduces FDs to their essential form.     **5.** **1NF** = atomic values. **2NF** = no partial dependency. **3NF** = no transitive dependency. **BCNF** = every determinant is a superkey.     **6.** **Lossless join** and **dependency preservation** are the two goals of decomposition. **3NF synthesis** achieves both; **BCNF decomposition** achieves only losslessness.

docs.title: Next — Chapter 5
docs.text:
Relational Algebra and Calculus.

- **σ, π, ×, ∪, −, ρ** — the six fundamental operations. - **Joins**: theta, equi, natural, outer. - **Division** — for "for all" queries. - **Tuple relational calculus (TRC)** and **domain relational calculus (DRC)**. - **Examples** on the COMPANY database. Chapter 4 gave a normalized schema. Chapter 5 gives the **query algebra** — the theoretical foundation of SQL.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text: 1. Express queries using the **six fundamental relational-algebra operations**.     2. Distinguish **theta, equi, natural**, and **outer** joins.     3. Use **division** for "for all" queries.     4. Translate between **relational algebra** and **tuple relational calculus**.     5. Translate between **TRC** and **domain relational calculus**.

docs.title: 5.1 — Why Relational Algebra?
docs.text:
Definition (Elmasri §6.1)

Relational algebra is a procedural query language: each query is a sequence of operations on relations, producing a new relation.

???+ info "Why it matters" - It is the **theoretical foundation** of SQL. - It is the **intermediate language** for query optimization — every SQL query is translated to a relational-algebra tree. - It is **relationally complete** — any query expressible in relational calculus can be expressed in relational algebra. !!! tip "Procedural vs declarative" Relational algebra is **procedural** — you specify the operations. Relational calculus (and SQL) is **declarative** — you specify what you want. The two are equivalent in power.

docs.title: 5.2 — The Six Fundamental Operations
docs.text: The minimal complete set Operation Symbol Arity Purpose Selection \(\sigma\) Unary Filter tuples Projection \(\pi\) Unary Select columns Union \(\cup\) Binary Combine two relations Difference \(-\) Binary Tuples in first but not second Cartesian product \(\times\) Binary All pairings Rename \(\rho\) Unary Rename relations/attributes   !!! tip "Everything else is derived"     Joins, intersection, division — all can be expressed using these six. Knowing which are *fundamental* is essential for understanding query optimization.

docs.title: 5.3 — Selection (\(\sigma\))
docs.text:
Definition

\(\sigma_{\text{condition}}(R)\) returns the tuples of \(R\) satisfying the boolean condition.

???+ info "Conditions" - Comparison: $=, \ne, <, \le, >, \ge$. - Boolean: $\land, \lor, \lnot$. - Attribute names and constants. ???+ info "Examples" - $\sigma_{\text{salary} > 40000}(\text{EMPLOYEE})$ — employees earning > 40k. - $\sigma_{\text{dno}=5 \land \text{sex}='F'}(\text{EMPLOYEE})$ — female employees in dept 5. !!! tip "Selection is commutative" $\sigma_{c_1}(\sigma_{c_2}(R)) = \sigma_{c_2}(\sigma_{c_1}(R))$. This is the first rule of query optimization.

docs.title: 5.4 — Projection (\(\pi\))
docs.text:
Definition

\(\pi_{A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_k}(R)\) returns a relation with only the listed attributes. Duplicates are removed — the result is a set.

???+ info "Examples" - $\pi_{\text{name, salary}}(\text{EMPLOYEE})$ — names and salaries. - $\pi_{\text{dno}}(\text{EMPLOYEE})$ — departments that have at least one employee (duplicates removed). !!! warning "Projection and duplicates" $\pi_{\text{dno}}(\text{EMPLOYEE})$ has **one tuple per department**, not per employee. This is because relational algebra is set-based. In SQL, you need `DISTINCT` because SQL's default is bag semantics.

docs.title: 5.5 — Union, Difference, Intersection
docs.text:
Set-theoretic operations

For \(R\) and \(S\) with the same schema (union-compatible):

  • \(R \cup S\) — tuples in \(R\) or \(S\) or both.
  • \(R - S\) — tuples in \(R\) but not \(S\).
  • \(R \cap S\) — tuples in both (derived: \(R - (R - S)\)).
???+ info "Union-compatibility" Both relations must have the **same number of attributes** and **compatible domains** in each position. Attribute names may differ. ???+ info "Example" Departments that have employees or projects: $$ \pi_{\text{dno}}(\text{EMPLOYEE}) \cup \pi_{\text{dnum}}(\text{PROJECT}). $$ !!! warning "Union removes duplicates" $R \cup S$ contains each tuple once. If you want to count duplicates, you need SQL's `UNION ALL` — not expressible in pure relational algebra.

docs.title: 5.6 — Cartesian Product (\(\times\))
docs.text:
Definition

\(R \times S\) pairs every tuple of \(R\) with every tuple of \(S\). If \(R\) has \(n\) tuples and \(S\) has \(m\), \(R \times S\) has \(n \times m\) tuples.

???+ info "Example" With 100 employees and 10 departments, `EMPLOYEE × DEPARTMENT` has 1,000 tuples — most of them meaningless (employees paired with unrelated departments). !!! tip "Cartesian product is the basis for joins" Every join is a Cartesian product followed by a selection. Query optimizers know this — and rarely materialize the full cross product. ???+ warning "Size explosion" Cross products grow multiplicatively. On large tables, they are catastrophic. Always filter or join instead.

docs.title: 5.7 — Joins
docs.text: Four kinds of join Join Symbol Condition Theta join \(R \bowtie_\theta S\) Any predicate \(\theta\) Equijoin \(R \bowtie_{A=B} S\) Equality on attributes Natural join \(R \bowtie S\) Equality on all common attributes, duplicates removed Outer join \(R ⟕ S\), etc. Preserves unmatched tuples   ???+ info "Example — theta join"     $$     \text{EMPLOYEE} \bowtie_{\text{salary} > 50000} \text{DEPARTMENT}     $$      Pairs every employee earning > 50k with every department (rarely useful).     ???+ info "Example — equijoin"     $$     \text{EMPLOYEE} \bowtie_{\text{dno} = \text{dnumber}} \text{DEPARTMENT}     $$      Correct pairing of employees with their departments.     ???+ info "Example — natural join"     $$     \text{EMPLOYEE} \bowtie \text{DEPARTMENT}     $$      Same as the equijoin above, but with duplicate `dno`/`dnumber` removed automatically.

docs.title: 5.8 — Outer Joins
docs.text:
Why outer joins?

A natural join drops tuples that have no match on the other side. The outer join preserves them, padding the missing side with NULLs.

???+ note "Three variants" | Variant | Symbol | Preserves | |---|---|---| | **Left outer** | $R ⟕ S$ | All of $R$ | | **Right outer** | $R ⟖ S$ | All of $S$ | | **Full outer** | $R ⟗ S$ | All of $R$ and $S$ | ???+ info "Example" $$ \text{EMPLOYEE} ⟕ \text{DEPARTMENT} $$ Includes employees **with no department** (their `dno` is NULL in the padded DEPARTMENT columns). A regular natural join would drop them. !!! tip "Outer join in SQL" SQL supports all three variants: `LEFT JOIN`, `RIGHT JOIN`, `FULL OUTER JOIN`. The default `INNER JOIN` is the natural join.

docs.title: 5.9 — Division (\(\div\))
docs.text:
Definition

For \(R(A, B)\) and \(S(B)\): \(R \div S\) returns the \(A\)-values in \(R\) that appear with every \(B\)-value in \(S\).

???+ info "Formal definition" $$ R \div S = \{ t[A] \mid \forall s \in S,\ \exists r \in R : r[A] = t[A] \land r[B] = s[B] \}. $$ ???+ info "In relational algebra" $$ R \div S = \pi_A(R) - \pi_A(\pi_A(R) \times S - R). $$ "All $A$-values minus those that miss at least one $B$." !!! tip "Division = 'for all'" Division answers the "**for all**" questions: employees who work on **all** projects; students who took **every** required course; suppliers who supply **every** part.

docs.title: Worked example 5.1 — Division on COMPANY
docs.text:
Problem:

Find employees who work on all projects.

???+ note "**Step 1 — schema.**" $\text{WORKS\_ON}(\text{essn}, \text{pno})$, $\text{PROJECT}(\text{pnumber})$. ??? info "**Step 2 — set up division.**" $$ \pi_{\text{essn}, \text{pno}}(\text{WORKS\_ON}) \div \pi_{\text{pnumber}}(\text{PROJECT}). $$ ??? info "**Step 3 — join with EMPLOYEE for names.**" $$ \pi_{\text{name}}\bigl(\text{EMPLOYEE} \bowtie (\pi_{\text{essn}, \text{pno}}(\text{WORKS\_ON}) \div \pi_{\text{pnumber}}(\text{PROJECT}))\bigr). $$ ??? success "**Interpretation.**" Employees whose `pno` set covers every `pnumber` in PROJECT. If a new project is added, only those who work on it are included — automatically.

docs.title: 5.10 — Additional Operations
docs.text: Derived operations Operation Symbol Definition Intersection \(\cap\) \(R \cap S = R - (R - S)\) Natural join \(\bowtie\) \(\pi_{\text{all}} (\sigma_{\text{equal common attrs}}(R \times S))\) Assignment \(:=\) Name an intermediate result Aggregate \(\mathcal{F}\) Count, sum, avg, min, max   ???+ info "Aggregate operator"     $\mathcal{G}_{\text{grouping attrs}} \mathcal{F}_{\text{agg}}(\text{relation})$:      $\mathcal{G}_{\text{dno}} \mathcal{F}_{\text{COUNT(ssn), AVG(salary)}}(\text{EMPLOYEE})$      Groups by department; counts employees; averages salaries.     !!! tip "Relational algebra is closed"     Every operation takes relations and returns relations — so operations compose freely.

docs.title: Worked example 5.2 — Five COMPANY queries
docs.text:
Company schema:

EMPLOYEE(ssn, name, salary, dno), DEPARTMENT(dnumber, dname, mgr_ssn), PROJECT(pnumber, pname, dnum), WORKS_ON(essn, pno, hours).

???+ note "**Q1 — names of employees in 'Research'**" $$ \pi_{\text{name}}\bigl(\text{EMPLOYEE} \bowtie \sigma_{\text{dname}=\text{'Research'}}(\text{DEPARTMENT})\bigr) $$ ??? info "**Q2 — names of employees who work on 'ProductX'**" $$ \pi_{\text{name}}\bigl(\text{EMPLOYEE} \bowtie \text{WORKS\_ON} \bowtie \sigma_{\text{pname}=\text{'ProductX'}}(\text{PROJECT})\bigr) $$ ??? info "**Q3 — employees who do not work on any project**" $$ \pi_{\text{name}}(\text{EMPLOYEE}) - \pi_{\text{name}}(\text{EMPLOYEE} \bowtie \text{WORKS\_ON}) $$ ??? info "**Q4 — department with the highest-paid manager**" Let $S := \mathcal{G}_{\text{dno}} \mathcal{F}_{\text{MAX(salary)}}(\text{EMPLOYEE})$. $$ \pi_{\text{dname}}\Bigl(\sigma_{\text{salary} = \text{max}}(\text{EMPLOYEE} \bowtie S) \bowtie \text{DEPARTMENT}\Bigr) $$ ??? info "**Q5 — employees who work on all projects**" $$ \pi_{\text{name}}\bigl(\text{EMPLOYEE} \bowtie (\pi_{\text{essn}, \text{pno}}(\text{WORKS\_ON}) \div \pi_{\text{pnumber}}(\text{PROJECT}))\bigr) $$

docs.title: 5.11 — Tuple Relational Calculus
docs.text:
Definition (Elmasri §6.6)

TRC is a declarative language: a query is a set of tuples satisfying a predicate.

\[ \{ t \mid P(t) \} \]

where \(t\) is a tuple variable.

???+ info "Quantifiers" - $\exists t \in R \; P(t)$ — there exists a tuple in $R$ satisfying $P$. - $\forall t \in R \; P(t)$ — every tuple in $R$ satisfies $P$. ???+ info "Example" Employees earning > 40k: $$ \{ t \mid t \in \text{EMPLOYEE} \land t[\text{salary}] > 40000 \}. $$ !!! tip "TRC is declarative" You specify **what** — not how. The DBMS decides the execution order. This is the same paradigm as SQL.

docs.title: Worked example 5.3 — TRC queries
docs.text:
Express in TRC:

???+ note "**Q1 — names of employees in 'Research'**" $$ \{ t[\text{name}] \mid t \in \text{EMPLOYEE} \land \exists d \in \text{DEPARTMENT} \; (d[\text{dnumber}] = t[\text{dno}] \land d[\text{dname}] = \text{'Research'}) \} $$ ??? info "**Q2 — employees who work on all projects**" $$ \{ t[\text{name}] \mid t \in \text{EMPLOYEE} \land \forall p \in \text{PROJECT} \; \exists w \in \text{WORKS\_ON} \; (w[\text{essn}] = t[\text{ssn}] \land w[\text{pno}] = p[\text{pnumber}]) \} $$ ??? info "**Q3 — departments with no employees**" $$ \{ d[\text{dname}] \mid d \in \text{DEPARTMENT} \land \lnot \exists e \in \text{EMPLOYEE} \; (e[\text{dno}] = d[\text{dnumber}]) \} $$ ??? success "**Notice the pattern.**" - "There exists" → $\exists$. - "For all" → $\forall$. - "Does not exist" → $\lnot \exists$.

docs.title: 5.12 — Domain Relational Calculus
docs.text:
Definition

DRC quantifies over domain values, not tuples.

\[ \{ \langle x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n \rangle \mid P(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \} \] ???+ info "Example" Employees earning > 40k: $$ \{ \langle n \rangle \mid \exists s, a, d \; (\text{EMPLOYEE}(s, n, a, d) \land a > 40000) \} $$ Note: `EMPLOYEE(s, n, a, d)` is a predicate asserting "there is a tuple with these values". !!! tip "TRC vs DRC" Both are **relationally complete** — they express the same set of queries. TRC is easier for large schemas (tuple variables); DRC is easier for formal proofs (pure first-order logic). ???+ warning "Safety" DRC expressions must be **safe** — every variable must be drawn from a finite domain. Without safety, expressions can range over infinite domains and produce infinite results.

docs.title: 5.13 — Equivalence of Languages
docs.text: Three equivalent languages Language Style Power Relational algebra Procedural Same Tuple relational calculus Declarative Same Domain relational calculus Declarative Same   ???+ abstract "Codd's theorem"     Relational algebra, TRC, and DRC are **relationally complete** — they express exactly the same set of queries (those expressible in first-order logic over finite relations).     !!! tip "Why this matters"     - **Query optimization**: converting SQL (calculus) to a plan (algebra).     - **Correctness proofs**: showing two queries are equivalent.     - **Language design**: SQL is essentially a syntactically sugared TRC.

docs.title: Chapter 5 — key takeaways
docs.text: **1.** Six **fundamental operations**: $\sigma, \pi, \cup, -, \times, \rho$. Everything else is derived.     **2.** **Selection** filters tuples; **projection** selects columns and **removes duplicates**.     **3.** **Joins**: theta (any predicate), equi (equality), natural (equality on common attrs), outer (preserves unmatched).     **4.** **Division** answers "for all" questions — employees who work on all projects.     **5.** **TRC** quantifies over tuples; **DRC** quantifies over values. Both are declarative.     **6.** **Codd's theorem**: relational algebra, TRC, and DRC are **relationally complete** — same expressive power.

docs.title: Next — Chapter 6
docs.text:
SQL.

- **DDL**: `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`; constraints. - **DML**: `SELECT` with `WHERE`, joins, aggregates, `GROUP BY`, `HAVING`, subqueries, `EXISTS`, set operations, `NULL` handling. - **Data modification**: `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`. Chapter 5 gave the **theory**. Chapter 6 gives the **language** every database engineer uses every day.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text: 1. Create schemas with **DDL**: `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, all constraint types.     2. Write **SELECT** queries with filtering, projection, joins, aggregates, subqueries.     3. Use **GROUP BY** and **HAVING** correctly.     4. Handle **NULL** semantics, set operations, and `EXISTS`.     5. Modify data with **INSERT**, **UPDATE**, **DELETE** while respecting constraints.

docs.title: 6.1 — Objectives of SQL
docs.text:
Design goals
  • Declarative — specify what, not how.
  • Universal — one syntax, every major DBMS.
  • Standardised — ANSI/ISO since 1986 (SQL-86, 92, 99, 2003, 2008, 2011, 2016, 2023).
  • Non-procedural — queries return sets, not loops.
???+ info "Two sublanguages" | Sublanguage | Purpose | Statements | |---|---|---| | **DDL** | Define / modify schema | `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP` | | **DML** | Query / modify data | `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` | !!! tip "SQL has three modes of execution" 1. **Interactive** — typed at a terminal. 2. **Embedded** — called from a host language (Java, Python). 3. **Dynamic** — constructed at runtime (ORM frameworks).

docs.title: 6.2 — DDL: Creating a Table
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE DEPARTMENT (
    dnumber INT PRIMARY KEY,
    dname   VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    mgr_ssn CHAR(9)
);
???+ note "The constraint vocabulary" | Constraint | Meaning | |---|---| | `PRIMARY KEY` | Uniquely identifies each tuple; **implies NOT NULL** | | `FOREIGN KEY` | Referential integrity | | `UNIQUE` | All values distinct (NULL allowed) | | `NOT NULL` | No NULL values | | `CHECK` | Boolean condition on each tuple | | `DEFAULT` | Default value if none provided | !!! warning "PRIMARY KEY implies UNIQUE + NOT NULL" You do not need to write both. `PRIMARY KEY` already enforces both.

docs.title: 6.3 — DDL: Foreign Keys
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE EMPLOYEE (
    ssn     CHAR(9) PRIMARY KEY,
    name    VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    salary  DECIMAL(10,2) CHECK (salary >= 0),
    dno     INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (dno) REFERENCES DEPARTMENT(dnumber)
        ON DELETE SET NULL
        ON UPDATE CASCADE
);
???+ note "Referential actions" | Action | On DELETE / UPDATE | |---|---| | `RESTRICT` / `NO ACTION` | Reject the operation (default) | | `CASCADE` | Propagate the change | | `SET NULL` | Set the foreign key to NULL | | `SET DEFAULT` | Set to default | ???+ info "Combining actions" You can specify different actions for delete and update: 
FOREIGN KEY (dno) REFERENCES DEPARTMENT(dnumber)
    ON DELETE SET NULL
    ON UPDATE CASCADE

docs.title: 6.4 — DDL: Circular References
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE DEPARTMENT (
    dnumber INT PRIMARY KEY,
    dname   VARCHAR(50),
    mgr_ssn CHAR(9)               -- no FK here yet
);

CREATE TABLE EMPLOYEE (
    ssn  CHAR(9) PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(50),
    dno  INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (dno) REFERENCES DEPARTMENT(dnumber)
);

ALTER TABLE DEPARTMENT
    ADD FOREIGN KEY (mgr_ssn) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(ssn);
!!! tip "The circular-reference pattern" - Create the first table **without** the foreign key. - Create the second table with its foreign key. - Add the first table's foreign key with `ALTER TABLE`. ???+ warning "The alternative — deferred constraints" Some DBMSes support `DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED` — the constraint is checked at commit time, not statement time. This allows circular references without ALTER.

docs.title: 6.5 — ALTER and DROP
docs.text:
ALTER TABLE EMPLOYEE ADD COLUMN email VARCHAR(100);
ALTER TABLE EMPLOYEE DROP COLUMN email;
ALTER TABLE EMPLOYEE ADD CONSTRAINT chk_salary CHECK (salary >= 1000);
ALTER TABLE EMPLOYEE DROP CONSTRAINT chk_salary;

DROP TABLE EMPLOYEE;                    -- fails if other tables reference it
DROP TABLE EMPLOYEE CASCADE;            -- drops dependent constraints too
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS EMPLOYEE;          -- no error if missing
!!! warning "ALTER with data present" Adding a `NOT NULL` column to a table with rows requires a **default value**: 
ALTER TABLE EMPLOYEE ADD COLUMN status VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active';
Without a default, the statement fails. ???+ info "DROP vs TRUNCATE vs DELETE" | Command | Removes | |---|---| | `DROP TABLE` | The table and all its data | | `TRUNCATE TABLE` | All rows, keeps the schema | | `DELETE FROM` | Selected rows |

docs.title: 6.6 — SELECT: The Basic Form
docs.text:
SELECT   column1, column2, ...
FROM     table1, table2, ...
WHERE    condition
GROUP BY grouping_columns
HAVING   group_condition
ORDER BY sort_columns;
???+ note "Logical evaluation order" 1. `FROM` — build the Cartesian product of the tables. 2. `WHERE` — filter tuples. 3. `GROUP BY` — group remaining tuples. 4. `HAVING` — filter groups. 5. `SELECT` — evaluate the projected columns. 6. `DISTINCT` — remove duplicate rows. 7. `ORDER BY` — sort the result. !!! warning "The evaluation order has consequences" - Aggregates cannot appear in `WHERE` (aggregation hasn't happened yet). - Column aliases defined in `SELECT` cannot be used in `WHERE`. - `ORDER BY` can use `SELECT` aliases.

docs.title: 6.7 — Basic SELECT Examples
docs.text:
-- All employees
SELECT * FROM EMPLOYEE;

-- Filter
SELECT ssn, name FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE salary > 40000;

-- Distinct departments
SELECT DISTINCT dno FROM EMPLOYEE;

-- Sort
SELECT name, salary FROM EMPLOYEE ORDER BY salary DESC, name ASC;

-- Alias
SELECT name AS employee_name FROM EMPLOYEE;
???+ info "`DISTINCT` vs no `DISTINCT`" - `SELECT dno FROM EMPLOYEE` — one row per employee (duplicates). - `SELECT DISTINCT dno FROM EMPLOYEE` — one row per department. !!! tip "SQL is bag semantics by default" Unlike relational algebra (set), SQL returns **bags** — duplicates preserved unless `DISTINCT` is specified. This is a frequent source of confusion.

docs.title: 6.8 — Joins in SQL
docs.text:
Four join syntaxes 
-- Implicit (old style)
SELECT e.name, d.dname
FROM   EMPLOYEE e, DEPARTMENT d
WHERE  e.dno = d.dnumber;

-- Explicit INNER JOIN
SELECT e.name, d.dname
FROM   EMPLOYEE e INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT d ON e.dno = d.dnumber;

-- LEFT JOIN (preserves employees with no dept)
SELECT e.name, d.dname
FROM   EMPLOYEE e LEFT JOIN DEPARTMENT d ON e.dno = d.dnumber;

-- NATURAL JOIN (equal common columns)
SELECT e.name, d.dname
FROM   EMPLOYEE e NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT d;
???+ info "Join types" | SQL | Equivalent to | |---|---| | `INNER JOIN` | Natural join / equijoin | | `LEFT JOIN` | Left outer join | | `RIGHT JOIN` | Right outer join | | `FULL OUTER JOIN` | Full outer join | !!! warning "Implicit join pitfall" Forgetting the `WHERE` clause in the old-style syntax produces a **Cartesian product** — for 1M employees × 1k departments, that's 10⁹ rows.

docs.title: 6.9 — Aggregates and GROUP BY
docs.text:
SELECT   dno, COUNT(*) AS n, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal
FROM     EMPLOYEE
GROUP BY dno
HAVING   COUNT(*) > 5;
???+ note "Aggregate functions" | Function | Returns | |---|---| | `COUNT(*)` | Number of rows | | `COUNT(col)` | Number of non-NULL values in `col` | | `SUM(col)` | Sum of non-NULL values | | `AVG(col)` | Average of non-NULL values | | `MIN(col)`, `MAX(col)` | Minimum, maximum | !!! warning "The GROUP BY rule" Every column in `SELECT` that is **not** an aggregate must appear in `GROUP BY`. Violating this is a syntax error in strict SQL mode and undefined behavior otherwise. ???+ info "WHERE vs HAVING" - `WHERE` filters **rows** before grouping. - `HAVING` filters **groups** after grouping. - `HAVING` can use aggregate functions; `WHERE` cannot.

docs.title: Worked example 6.1 — Aggregates
docs.text:
Problem:

For each department, list dname, number of employees, and average salary, but only for departments with more than 5 employees and average salary ≥ 40,000.

???+ note "**Step 1 — the query.**" 
SELECT   d.dname, COUNT(*) AS n, AVG(e.salary) AS avg_sal
FROM     DEPARTMENT d JOIN EMPLOYEE e ON e.dno = d.dnumber
GROUP BY d.dnumber, d.dname
HAVING   COUNT(*) > 5 AND AVG(e.salary) >= 40000;
??? info "**Step 2 — why `d.dnumber` is in `GROUP BY`.**" `dname` is functionally determined by `dnumber`, so grouping by both is valid. Strictly, grouping by `dnumber` alone is enough (in PostgreSQL, you can omit `dname`), but grouping by both is portable. ??? success "**Step 3 — the semantics.**" - `JOIN` pairs employees with their departments. - `GROUP BY` groups employees per department. - `HAVING` discards departments that fail either condition.

docs.title: 6.10 — Subqueries
Worked example 6.2 — Subquery problems
docs.text:
Problems:

???+ note "**Q1 — employees earning above the company average**" 
SELECT name FROM EMPLOYEE
WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM EMPLOYEE);
??? info "**Q2 — employees earning above their department average**" 
SELECT name FROM EMPLOYEE e
WHERE salary > (
    SELECT AVG(salary) FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE dno = e.dno
);
??? info "**Q3 — highest-paid employee in each department**" 
SELECT dno, name, salary FROM EMPLOYEE e
WHERE salary = (
    SELECT MAX(salary) FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE dno = e.dno
);
??? info "**Q4 — employees who work on at least one project**" 
SELECT name FROM EMPLOYEE e
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM WORKS_ON w WHERE w.essn = e.ssn);
??? info "**Q5 — employees who work on no projects**" 
SELECT name FROM EMPLOYEE e
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM WORKS_ON w WHERE w.essn = e.ssn);

docs.title: 6.11 — EXISTS, IN, ANY, ALL
6.12 — Set Operations
docs.text:
Three set operators Operator Meaning Duplicates UNION Combine two results Removed UNION ALL Combine two results Preserved INTERSECT Rows in both Removed EXCEPT / MINUS Rows in first not second Removed ???+ info "Example" 
SELECT ssn FROM EMPLOYEE
UNION
SELECT mgr_ssn FROM DEPARTMENT;

SELECT ssn FROM EMPLOYEE
INTERSECT
SELECT essn FROM WORKS_ON;
!!! tip "UNION ALL is faster" `UNION` sorts or hashes to remove duplicates; `UNION ALL` simply concatenates. Use `ALL` when duplicates are impossible or irrelevant.

docs.title: 6.13 — NULL Semantics
6.14 — String Operations
docs.text:
LIKE pattern matching Pattern Matches 'A%' Starts with A '%a' Ends with a '%abc%' Contains abc '_bc' Any char, then bc ???+ info "Example" 
SELECT name FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE name LIKE 'A%';    -- starts with A
SELECT name FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE name LIKE '%son';  -- ends with son
SELECT name FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE name LIKE '_ob';   -- one char + "ob"
???+ info "Other string functions" 
SUBSTRING(name, 1, 3)          -- first 3 chars
UPPER(name), LOWER(name)       -- case
LENGTH(name)                   -- length
TRIM(name)                     -- strip whitespace
CONCAT(first, ' ', last)       -- concatenation

docs.title: 6.15 — INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
Worked example 6.3 — Data modification
docs.text:
Problem:

Give every employee in department 5 a 10% raise, and delete all employees in department 99.

???+ note "**Step 1 — the raise.**" 
UPDATE EMPLOYEE
SET    salary = salary * 1.10
WHERE  dno = 5;
The `WHERE` is **essential** — without it, all employees get the raise. ??? info "**Step 2 — the deletion.**" 
DELETE FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE dno = 99;
If `EMPLOYEE` has foreign keys to `WORKS_ON` or `DEPENDENT` with `RESTRICT`, this fails — you must first delete dependent rows (or use `ON DELETE CASCADE`). ??? success "**Step 3 — transaction safety.**" 
BEGIN;
UPDATE EMPLOYEE SET salary = salary * 1.10 WHERE dno = 5;
DELETE FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE dno = 99;
COMMIT;
Wrap multi-statement operations in a transaction so they either all succeed or all roll back.

docs.title: 6.16 — Views
docs.text:
Definition

A view is a named, stored query that behaves like a table.

???+ info "Example" 
CREATE VIEW HIGH_EARNERS AS
SELECT ssn, name, salary
FROM   EMPLOYEE
WHERE  salary > 100000;

SELECT * FROM HIGH_EARNERS;  -- query the view
???+ info "Why views?" - **Security** — expose only a subset of the data. - **Simplicity** — encapsulate complex joins. - **Logical data independence** — change the underlying schema without breaking apps that use the view. !!! warning "Updatable views" Simple views (no aggregates, no joins, no DISTINCT) are **updatable** — you can INSERT/UPDATE through them. Complex views are **read-only**.

docs.title: 6.17 — Indexes and Query Plans
Chapter 6 — key takeaways
docs.text: **1.** **DDL** creates/modifies the schema: `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP` with constraints (`PRIMARY KEY`, `FOREIGN KEY`, `UNIQUE`, `NOT NULL`, `CHECK`).     **2.** **SELECT** evaluation order: `FROM` → `WHERE` → `GROUP BY` → `HAVING` → `SELECT` → `DISTINCT` → `ORDER BY`. Aggregates cannot appear in `WHERE`.     **3.** **Joins**: `INNER`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `FULL OUTER`, and `NATURAL`. Forgetting the join condition produces a Cartesian product.     **4.** **Aggregates** (`COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`) with `GROUP BY` and `HAVING` — the pattern for summary queries.     **5.** **NULL** semantics: three-valued logic; `NULL = NULL` is UNKNOWN; use `IS NULL`. Watch for the `NOT IN` + `NULL` trap.     **6.** **INSERT**, **UPDATE**, **DELETE** respect constraints and referential actions. Wrap multi-statement operations in transactions.

docs.title: Next — Chapter 7
docs.text:
Disk Storage, File Structures, and Hashing.

- Disk structure and access time. - Files of records; slotted pages. - **Heap**, **sorted**, **hashed** file organizations. - **Static**, **dynamic**, **extendible** hashing. - **RAID** levels 0–6. Chapters 1–6 described the **logical** and **query** levels.

docs.title: Chapter 7 — Disk Storage, File Structures, and Hashing
Learning outcomes
docs.text: 1. Describe the **physical structure** of magnetic and solid-state storage.     2. Compute **disk access time** (seek + rotation + transfer) for a given workload.     3. Design **file organizations**: heap, sorted, hashed.     4. Explain **static, dynamic, and extendible hashing** and their trade-offs.     5. Choose an appropriate **RAID level** for a given workload.

docs.title: 7.1 — Disk Storage: Physical Structure
docs.text:
Magnetic hard disk (HDD) 
Platter (rotates at 5400–15000 RPM)
  │
  ├── Tracks (concentric circles)
  │     │
  │     └── Sectors (fixed-size blocks, ~512 B–4 KB)
  │
  └── Read/write head per surface
???+ note "Access time components" | Component | Typical value | Cause | |---|---|---| | **Seek** | 3–10 ms | Move the head to the right track | | **Rotation** | 2–6 ms (half a revolution) | Wait for the sector to rotate under | | **Transfer** | 0.03–0.2 ms (per block) | Read the data | !!! warning "Seek dominates" For random access, seek + rotation is 100–500× the transfer time. This is why **disk scheduling** (Chapter 8 of OS) and **B-tree indexing** exist — both reduce the number of seeks. ???+ note "Solid-state drive (SSD)" - NAND flash cells, no moving parts. - **No seek, no rotation.** - Random access ≈ 50–100 µs (vs. ~10 ms for HDD). - Finite write cycles (~10⁴–10⁵ per cell); wear-leveling firmware.

docs.title: 7.2 — File Organization
docs.text:
What is a file?

A file is a sequence of records stored on disk. Each record consists of fields (attributes).

???+ note "Three fundamental organizations" | Organization | Insert | Search by key | Range query | |---|---|---|---| | **Heap** | $O(1)$ | $O(b)$ full scan | $O(b)$ | | **Sorted** | $O(b)$ | $O(\log_2 b)$ binary search | $O(\log b + \text{matches})$ | | **Hashed** | $O(1)$ | $O(1)$ average | $O(b)$ (destroys order) | !!! tip "The choice depends on the workload" - **Heap** — if most queries scan the whole file. - **Sorted** — if range queries and ordered scans dominate. - **Hashed** — if point lookups dominate and range queries are rare.

docs.title: Worked example 7.1 — Disk access time
docs.text:
Problem:

HDD with 9 ms seek, 7200 RPM, 150 MB/s transfer. Compute the time to read a 4 KB block.

???+ note "**Step 1 — rotational latency.**" One revolution: $60 / 7200 = 8.333$ ms. Average latency: half a revolution = **4.17 ms**. ??? info "**Step 2 — transfer time.**" $$ T_{\text{transfer}} = \frac{4096}{150 \times 10^6} \approx 0.027\ \text{ms}. $$ ??? success "**Step 3 — total.**" $$ T = 9 + 4.17 + 0.027 \approx \mathbf{13.2\ \text{ms per block}}. $$ **IOPS** $\approx 1 / 0.0132 \approx \mathbf{76}$. ??? tip "**Comparison with SSD.**" SSD random read: ~50–100 µs = **~0.075 ms**. That's **175× faster** than the HDD above. Random-access workloads (databases, VM) hit this difference hardest.

docs.title: 7.3 — Fixed vs Variable-Length Records
docs.text:
Fixed-length records
  • Every record has the same size.
  • Direct access: address = file_start + record_size × record_number.
  • Simple but wastes space (padding).
???+ note "Variable-length records" - Records differ in length (e.g., a `VARCHAR` field). - **Slotted page** structure: a header, a slot directory, and variable-length record data. ???+ info "Slotted page layout" 
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│  Header (record count, free ptr) │
├─────────────────────────────────┤
│  Slot 1 → offset                 │
│  Slot 2 → offset                 │
│  ...                             │
├─────────────────────────────────┤
│  Free space                      │
├─────────────────────────────────┤
│  Record N                        │
│  Record ...                      │
│  Record 1                        │
└─────────────────────────────────┘
The slot directory points to record offsets. Records can move within the page without affecting external pointers.

docs.title: 7.4 — Static Hashing
docs.text:
Definition

A hash file uses a hash function \(h(k)\) to map a key to a bucket (typically one disk block). All records with the same hash go to the same bucket.

???+ note "Static hashing" - The number of buckets $M$ is fixed at creation. - $h(k) = k \bmod M$. - **Problem:** if $M$ is too small, overflow chains grow. - If $M$ is too large, most buckets are empty. !!! warning "The overflow problem" When a bucket is full, new records go to an **overflow block** chained from the primary. As the file grows, chains lengthen, and search degrades from $O(1)$ to $O(n)$. ???+ info "Example" $M = 5$, keys $\{10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35\}$, $h(k) = k \bmod 5$. | Bucket | Keys | |---|---| | 0 | 10, 20, 30 | | 1 | — | | 2 | — | | 3 | 15, 25, 35 | | 4 | — | Buckets 0 and 3 hold multiple records — overflow if capacity is less than 3.

docs.title: 7.5 — Dynamic Hashing
docs.text:
Why dynamic hashing?

Static hashing cannot grow or shrink gracefully. Dynamic hashing adjusts the number of buckets as the file grows.

???+ note "Two main variants" | Variant | Structure | Growth | |---|---|---| | **Extendible hashing** | Directory + buckets | Doubles directory when needed | | **Linear hashing** | No directory | Splits one bucket at a time | !!! tip "The trade-off" - Extendible hashing has **$O(1)$ search** (via directory) but pays for directory maintenance. - Linear hashing has **no directory** but may probe more than one bucket during splits.

docs.title: 7.6 — Extendible Hashing
docs.text:
The structure
  • Directory — an array of \(2^d\) pointers, where \(d\) is the global depth.
  • Buckets — hold the actual records; each has a local depth \(d_i\).
  • To find a record: use the first \(d\) bits of \(h(k)\) to index the directory.
???+ note "Splitting a bucket" When a bucket overflows: 1. If local depth $d_i < d$: increment $d_i$, split the bucket's records into two by the next bit, update directory pointers. 2. If local depth $d_i = d$: double the directory (increment $d$), then split. ???+ info "Search cost" - **Directory lookup:** $O(1)$. - **Bucket access:** $O(1)$. - Total: **$O(1)$** — no overflow chains.

docs.title: Worked example 7.2 — Extendible hashing insert
docs.text:
Problem:

Start with \(d = 2\) (4 directory entries). Buckets contain keys \(\{0, 4\}\), \(\{1, 5\}\), \(\{2, 6\}\), \(\{3, 7\}\). Bucket capacity = 2. Insert key 12.

???+ note "**Step 1 — hash 12.**" Assume $h(12) = 12$ (mod some power of 2). Binary: `1100`. First 2 bits: `11` → directory index 3. ??? info "**Step 2 — bucket 3 is full.**" Bucket 3 currently holds $\{3, 7\}$ (local depth 2 = global depth). ??? info "**Step 3 — split requires doubling the directory.**" Global depth becomes 3. Directory grows to 8 entries. Bucket 3's local depth becomes 3. Split $\{3, 7, 12\}$ by the third bit: - `011` → bucket for 3 - `111` → bucket for 7, 12 (if capacity > 2, they stay; else split again). ??? success "**Result.**" The directory doubled; buckets redistributed by one extra bit. **No overflow chains.** Search remains $O(1)$.

docs.title: 7.7 — Linear Hashing
docs.text:
The idea

No directory. A split pointer moves through the buckets, splitting one bucket at a time when the load factor exceeds a threshold.

???+ note "The algorithm" - Buckets numbered $0, \ldots, M-1$, with a **level** $L$. - Insert uses $h_L(k) = k \bmod (M \cdot 2^L)$. - When load factor > threshold, split bucket at the split pointer (using $h_{L+1}$), then advance the pointer. - When the pointer reaches the end, increment $L$ and reset the pointer. ???+ info "Trade-offs" | Aspect | Extendible | Linear | |---|---|---| | Directory | Yes | No | | Search | Always $O(1)$ | Usually $O(1)$, may need 2 lookups during split | | Space overhead | Directory | Minimal | | Simplicity | Moderate | Complex logic | !!! tip "Which is used in practice?" Most production systems use **B-trees** rather than hashing for their primary index — because B-trees support range queries. Hashing wins for **point lookups only** (e.g., in-memory caches, key-value stores like Redis).

docs.title: 7.8 — RAID: The Idea
docs.text:
Definition

RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) combines multiple physical disks into a single logical unit for performance, reliability, or both.

???+ note "Two fundamental techniques" - **Striping** — split data across disks (performance). - **Mirroring / parity** — duplicate data (reliability). !!! warning "RAID is not backup" RAID protects against **disk failure**, not against accidental deletion, corruption, ransomware, or site loss. Backup is a separate concern.

docs.title: 7.9 — RAID Levels 0–6
