docs.text: The main levels Level Technique Redundancy Performance Storage efficiency RAID 0 Striping None Fastest 100% RAID 1 Mirroring Full Fast read, slow write 50% RAID 2 Bit striping + Hamming ECC Yes Medium Low RAID 3 Byte striping + dedicated parity 1 disk Medium \(\frac{n-1}{n}\) RAID 4 Block striping + dedicated parity 1 disk Medium \(\frac{n-1}{n}\) RAID 5 Block striping + distributed parity 1 disk Good read, slower write \(\frac{n-1}{n}\) RAID 6 Block striping + double parity 2 disks Good read, slower write \(\frac{n-2}{n}\)   !!! tip "The practical winners"     - **RAID 0** — scratch space, no durability needed.     - **RAID 1** — small servers, two disks.     - **RAID 5** — general-purpose storage, read-heavy.     - **RAID 6** — large arrays, write-tolerant.     - **RAID 10** (not in the standard list) — mirror + stripe, best performance + reliability, 50% storage.     !!! warning "RAID 5 write penalty"     Every write requires **read-modify-write** of the parity block — the bottleneck for write-heavy workloads. RAID 10 avoids this; that's why databases often prefer it.

docs.title: Worked example 7.3 — Choose a RAID level
docs.text:
Problem:

Match each scenario to a RAID level.

???+ note "**Scenario A — 10 TB backup server, sequential writes, cost matters.**" **RAID 6.** Two-disk redundancy, ~67% storage efficiency, tolerates large-disk rebuilds. ??? info "**Scenario B — OLTP database, read-heavy, frequent small writes.**" **RAID 10.** Fast reads (mirror), avoids RAID 5's parity write penalty, 50% storage. ??? info "**Scenario C — video editing scratch space, no persistence needed.**" **RAID 0.** Maximum throughput, no durability required (data regenerated). ??? info "**Scenario D — home NAS, four 4 TB disks, mixed read/write.**" **RAID 5.** 75% storage (12 TB usable), tolerates one disk failure, good read performance. ??? success "**The rule of thumb.**" - Performance → RAID 0 or 10. - Capacity → RAID 5. - Safety at scale → RAID 6. - Small/cheap → RAID 1.

docs.title: 7.10 — Buffering and Caching
docs.text:
The disk is slow

Disk latency is ~100,000× CPU speed. The DBMS hides this with memory:

???+ note "Three layers" | Layer | Where | What it caches | |---|---|---| | **Buffer pool** | DBMS memory | Recently used disk pages | | **OS page cache** | OS kernel | File-system pages | | **On-disk cache** | Disk controller | Pre-fetched sectors | ???+ info "Replacement policies" - **LRU** — evict least-recently used page. - **Clock** — approximate LRU using a reference bit. - **LRU-K** — evict page with oldest $K$-th most recent access. - **ARC** — adaptive; balances recency and frequency. !!! tip "The buffer pool is the DBMS's most valuable resource" All query performance depends on it. Tuning its size and replacement policy is one of the DBA's most important jobs.

docs.title: Chapter 7 — key takeaways
docs.text: **1.** Disk access time = **seek + rotation + transfer**. Seek dominates — this is why disk scheduling and indexing exist.     **2.** **File organizations**: heap (fast insert, slow search), sorted (fast search, slow insert), hashed (fast point lookup, no order).     **3.** **Static hashing** has overflow chains that grow. **Dynamic hashing** (extendible, linear) grows gracefully.     **4.** **Extendible hashing** uses a directory; **linear hashing** uses a split pointer and no directory.     **5.** **RAID 0** = performance only, **RAID 1** = mirror, **RAID 5** = distributed parity (1-failure), **RAID 6** = double parity (2-failures).     **6.** **Buffer pools** and **caches** are the DBMS's defence against the 100,000× speed gap between CPU and disk.

docs.title: Course wrap-up
docs.text: **The arc of ECEG-4191:**  1. **Chapter 1** — what a DBMS is, and why file-based systems fail. 2. **Chapter 2** — the relational model: relations, keys, constraints. 3. **Chapter 3** — conceptual design: ER/EER modelling. 4. **Chapter 4** — logical design: ER-to-relational mapping and normalization. 5. **Chapter 5** — relational algebra and calculus: the theoretical query language. 6. **Chapter 6** — SQL: the practical query language. 7. **Chapter 7** — storage and file structures: where the data lives.     !!! tip "The unifying question"     Every chapter asked: **how do we represent, design, query, and store data so that it is consistent, efficient, and evolvable?**      - **Represent** — the relational model.     - **Design** — ER modelling and normalization.     - **Query** — relational algebra and SQL.     - **Store** — file organizations, hashing, RAID.     **Good luck with the exam.**
